question: Storage of vaccines in the community: weak link in the cold chain?
answer: Yes. In a survey of community practices in Manchester and Bradford, only 16 of 40 respondents knew the appropriate storage conditions, and in six of eight monitored practices the refrigerators exposed vaccines to subzero temperatures or temperatures up to 16 degrees C. Few practices had adequate temperature monitoring: eight of the 40 respondents had minimum/maximum thermometers, and only one of these was checked daily. Stakeholder interviews in six countries likewise recognized heat and freeze exposure of vaccines as challenges (heat the greater concern). Freeze exposure was linked to ice build-up from poor refrigerator performance (reported by 53%) and improper icepack conditioning (28%). Ontario physicians identified problems with storage and handling as one of the barriers to using varicella vaccine.

question: Should general practitioners call patients by their first names?
answer: In a survey of 475 patients in Lothian general practices, most either liked (223) or did not mind (175) being called by their first names, while only 77 disliked it, so first-name use by GPs is acceptable to most patients. Those who disliked being addressed by first name were mostly aged over 65, so older patients may be less comfortable with it. Most patients (324) did not want to call their doctor by the doctor's first name, so the acceptability seen for doctors using patients' first names does not extend to the reverse.

question: Cardiopulmonary bypass temperature does not affect postoperative euthyroid sick syndrome?
answer: In a small prospective study of 12 cardiac surgery patients, hypothermic (26°C) and normothermic (35°C) CPB produced the same pattern of postoperative thyroid changes, consistent with euthyroid sick syndrome, so CPB temperature did not appear to affect it. In both temperature groups, total T4 and T3 fell below baseline from the start of CPB and stayed low for up to 5 days. Free T3 was reduced for up to 3 days, reverse T3 was elevated on postoperative days 1 and 3, and TSH was unchanged. The cold and warm CPB groups were comparable in age, weight, CPB duration, cross-clamp time, inotrope use, hospital stay, and postoperative outcomes such as myocardial infarction, heart failure, and death.

question: Does continuous intravenous infusion of low-concentration epinephrine impair uterine blood flow in pregnant ewes?
answer: In 10 near-term gravid ewes, continuous intravenous infusion of bupivacaine containing epinephrine at 1:200,000, 1:400,000 or 1:800,000 for 60 minutes had no effect on uterine blood flow or any other measured maternal or fetal hemodynamic variable. In contrast, a single intravenous bolus of epinephrine 15 micrograms in the same ewes reduced uterine blood flow to about 68 +/- 14% of baseline.

question: Substance use and HIV-related sexual behaviors among US high school students: are they related?
answer: In a nationally representative 1990 survey of 11,631 US high school students, substance use was associated with HIV-related sexual risk behaviors: non-users were least likely to have had intercourse, had four or more partners, or not used a condom at last intercourse, and odds ratios were greatest among marijuana, cocaine, or other illicit drug users. Even students who used only alcohol or cigarettes had smaller but still significant increases in the likelihood of having had sexual intercourse and of having four or more sex partners. In a separate analysis of 1991 YRBS data on white and Asian/Pacific Islander students, use of alcohol or other drugs before sex was significantly related to condom use.

question: Do family physicians make good sentinels for influenza?
answer: Volunteer family physician sentinel reports usefully supplemented CDC influenza surveillance over five seasons (1987-88 through 1991-92): physicians reported peak morbidity 1 to 4 weeks earlier than state and territorial health departments in four of five seasons. Sentinel physicians' influenza virus isolates peaked 1 to 4 weeks earlier than those reported by WHO laboratories, and in three of five seasons physicians obtained isolates from a greater proportion of specimens (36% vs 12%). Physician-reported peak morbidity preceded peak pneumonia and influenza mortality reported by 121 cities by 2 to 5 weeks in seasons with excess mortality, and the reports captured substantial burden (5% of office visits attributed to ILI; 43% of ILI hospitalizations in persons 65 and older).

question: Ultrasound in squamous cell carcinoma of the penis; a useful addition to clinical staging?
answer: Ultrasound appears to be a useful addition to clinical staging of penile squamous cell carcinoma: in 17 examined patients all tumors appeared as hypoechoic lesions, and ultrasound clearly showed whether the tunica albuginea of the corpus cavernosum was invaded. Ultrasound had limited accuracy for some staging details: in the glans region it could not distinguish subepithelial invasion from corpus spongiosum invasion, and it measured maximum tumor thickness accurately in only 7 of 16 examinations.

question: Must early postoperative oral intake be limited to laparoscopy?
answer: Early oral intake is not limited to laparoscopy: in a randomized trial of 190 open elective colorectal operations, immediate oral feeding was tolerated by 79.6% of patients in the first 4 days, with similar complication rates (17.3% vs 19.3%) to conventional feeding. A second randomized trial of 64 patients after open laparotomy with colonic or ileal resection found early regular feeding on the first postoperative morning feasible, with no difference in ileus duration (3.6 vs 3.4 days) and a trend toward shorter hospital stay (6.7 vs 8.0 days) in those who did not need nasogastric tube reinsertion.

question: Is the breast best for children with a family history of atopy?
answer: In a historic cohort of 794 children with a family history of atopy, breast-feeding was associated with lower illness rates in both the first year and the first three years of life. In the first year of life, breast-fed children with a family history of atopy had fewer episodes of gastroenteritis, lower respiratory tract infections, and digestive tract disorders. Over the following years they had fewer respiratory tract infections and skin infections. Broader survey data from 7092 US infants (not selected for atopy) showed a dose-related protective pattern. Full breast-feeding was linked to lower odds of diarrhea, cough or wheeze, and vomiting compared with no breast-feeding, and the findings did not vary by income.

question: The insertion allele of the ACE gene I/D polymorphism. A candidate gene for insulin resistance?
answer: In the one study that directly tested ACE I/D genotype against insulin resistance, the association appeared only in NIDDM subjects, and it ran toward the deletion allele: DD subjects had lower insulin levels and higher HOMA insulin sensitivity than II subjects. This does not support the insertion allele as a risk candidate. In 533 nondiabetic subjects, the same study found no differences in insulin sensitivity, insulin-like molecules, blood pressure, PAI-1, lipids, or CHD prevalence across ACE genotypes. Even among NIDDM subjects, genotype was not associated with CHD prevalence, blood pressure, serum lipids, or PAI-1 activity.

question: Prognosis of well differentiated small hepatocellular carcinoma--is well differentiated hepatocellular carcinoma clinically early cancer?
answer: In a cohort of 76 patients with solitary HCC up to 3 cm who underwent hepatectomy, well differentiated HCC did not show a better prognosis than less differentiated HCC: disease-free survival did not differ significantly between the groups, so it does not appear to be clinically early cancer. Well differentiated HCCs did not differ significantly from less differentiated HCCs in intrahepatic metastasis or portal vein invasion, although they had less fibrous capsule formation. Microscopic cancer cell infiltration into the fibrous frame of the portal tract was seen in a well differentiated HCC specimen, and tumor volume doubling time analysis of recurrent foci suggested that minute cancerous foci were already present at the time of surgery.

question: Does gestational age misclassification explain the difference in birthweights for Australian aborigines and whites?
answer: Gestational age misclassification does not appear to explain the birthweight divergence between Australian Aborigines and whites: in simulations, only extreme types of misclassification removed the divergence in median birthweights. At full term, birthweight distribution parameters were robust to gestational age misclassification, and at preterm the 10th centiles were robust as well. The 90th centiles at preterm gestations were sensitive to even minor misclassification, so misclassification could affect some upper-tail measures.

question: Biliary atresia: should all patients undergo a portoenterostomy?
answer: The evidence does not clearly support (or refute) portoenterostomy for all patients: outcomes after Kasai are variable, and in one study of 31 patients, preoperative histology on needle biopsy predicted surgical success in 27 of 31 (sensitivity 86%, specificity 88%), suggesting a more selective approach might be possible. In that same study, success after portoenterostomy could not be reliably predicted by gender, age at Kasai, or preoperative bilirubin or albumin levels, while syncitial giant cells, lobular inflammation, focal necrosis, bridging necrosis and cholangitis were each associated with failure. Some children benefit substantially from portoenterostomy: in a single-center series of 244 children operated on, 28 (11%) had normal laboratory indices and no clinical chronic liver disease 10 or more years later, and 93% of those were in mainstream education.

question: Does fluoridation reduce the use of dental services among adults?
answer: In a 2-year follow-up of 972 Washington state adults aged 20-34, those with lifetime fluoridated water exposure of half or more of their lives had less baseline disease and a lower but statistically nonsignificant probability of receiving a restoration. When only teeth with decay or unsatisfactory fillings at baseline were considered, adults with high fluoridation exposure had a lower probability of receiving a restoration than unexposed adults, indicating reduced restorative demand in that subset. Adults in the fluoridated community with a large dentist supply received more restorations than adults in the nonfluoridated community, suggesting possible supplier-induced demand that could offset reductions in service use.

question: Multidisciplinary breast cancer clinics. Do they work?
answer: A multidisciplinary breast cancer clinic was associated with higher patient satisfaction (greater involvement of family and friends, help with treatment decisions; P<0.001) and a shorter time from diagnosis to treatment start (42.2 vs 29.6 days; P<0.0008) compared with traditional sequential consultation. In a breast unit, 91.5% of 3230 multidisciplinary team decisions were concordant with subsequent management, and most discordant decisions were justifiable (e.g., patient choice or new information), suggesting that team decisions are generally implemented. Among older women, preoperative radiation oncology consultation was associated with much higher odds of breast-conserving surgery with radiation (OR 6.7) and of receiving radiation after breast-conserving surgery (OR 5), though only 29% had such a consultation.

question: Laparoscopic-assisted ileocolic resections in patients with Crohn's disease: are abscesses, phlegmons, or recurrent disease contraindications?
answer: In a series of 46 attempted laparoscopic-assisted ileocolic resections for Crohn's disease, patients with a preoperative abscess/phlegmon or recurrent disease at a prior anastomosis could be treated laparoscopically, so these factors were not found to be contraindications. Conversion to open surgery occurred in 1 of 14 (7%) patients with abscess/phlegmon and 2 of 10 (20%) with recurrent disease, versus 2 of 22 (9%) in uncomplicated disease. The laparoscopic groups had less blood loss, shorter operative times, lower morbidity (0% and 10% in the abscess/phlegmon and recurrent groups), and shorter hospital stays than 70 consecutive open resections (morbidity 21%, stay 7.9 days).

question: Does occupational nuclear power plant radiation affect conception and pregnancy?
answer: In a retrospective pair-matched study of 270 infertile couples, nuclear power plant exposure was no more frequent among infertile couples than among fertile controls, so occupational exposure was not associated with reduced fecundity. Nuclear power plant workers had a higher rate of anomalous spermiograms, but the abnormalities were temporary and did not correlate with cumulative equivalent radiation dose.

question: Does psychological distress predict disability?
answer: In a 10-year cohort of 8655 Finnish farmers, those in the highest quartile of baseline psychological distress had higher risk of disability pension overall (RR 1.76, 95% CI 1.44-2.14) than those in the lowest quartile, after adjustment for age, sex, smoking and BMI. The association held for several specific causes of disability: myocardial infarction (RR 2.34), depression (RR 2.50), neck-shoulder disorders (RR 1.98) and unspecified low-back disorders (RR 1.76). The association was not clear for knee osteoarthritis (RR 1.55, CI 0.91-2.63) or hip osteoarthritis (RR 0.89, CI 0.42-1.85), whose confidence intervals included 1.

question: Does the Child Health Computing System adequately identify children with cerebral palsy?
answer: The Child Health Computing System did not adequately identify children with cerebral palsy: 47% of the 135 cases on the Northern Ireland Cerebral Palsy Register were not found on the CHCS. question: Do general practitioner hospitals reduce the utilisation of general hospital beds?
answer: Populations with access to GP hospitals used general hospitals less: in Finnmark, admission rates were 26% (men) and 28% (women) lower, and occupied bed days 38% and 52% lower, in peripheral municipalities with a GP hospital than in central municipalities without one. The differences were most pronounced for respiratory diseases, cardiac failure and cancer (treated or cared for in GP hospitals) and for stroke and fractures (transferred to GP hospitals for follow-up care). GPs with access to a GP hospital referred a lower proportion of patients to general hospitals, with the GP hospital option mainly chosen because of distance, nursing needs and patient/family preferences.

question: Autoxidation products of both carbohydrates and lipids are increased in uremic plasma: is there oxidative stress in uremia?
answer: Uremic plasma showed elevated levels of protein adducts from both carbohydrate autoxidation (pentosidine) and lipid peroxidation (MDA-lysine), along with CML, which can derive from either source. question: Is HIV/STD control in Jamaica making a difference?
answer: The Jamaican HIV/STD Control Program was associated with favorable trends: AIDS incidence rose only marginally over three years (18.5 to 21.4 per 100,000 by 1997), HIV prevalence in general population groups stayed at about 1% or less, and syphilis and congenital syphilis declined. Reported sexual behaviour changed in protective directions: men aged 15-49 reporting sex with a non-regular partner fell from 35% (1994) to 26% (1996), and women's condom use with non-regular partners rose from 37% (1992) to 73% (1996). Condom use rose among gay men, inner-city adults and adolescents aged 12-14, and condom sales and distribution grew from about 2 million in 1985 to 10 million in 1995.

question: Is laparoscopic reoperation for failed antireflux surgery feasible?
answer: Laparoscopic reoperation after failed antireflux surgery appears feasible: in a 46-patient case series it was completed laparoscopically in most patients (20% overall conversion, 0% in the last 10), with no mortality, a mean hospital stay of 2.3 days, and improved well-being scores. In a prospective study of 20 patients with failed primary open antireflux surgery, 90% of laparoscopic refundoplications were completed laparoscopically, with 2 conversions to open surgery. Objective and quality-of-life outcomes improved after laparoscopic refundoplication: LES pressure rose from 6.08 to 11.9 mmHg, DeMeester score fell from 69.8 to 14.6, and GIQLI rose from 84.9 to 120.1 at 1 year. Satisfaction was high after laparoscopic reoperation: 89% of the 35 patients followed up were satisfied with their decision to have reoperation. The procedure carries notable technical demands and morbidity: operations took about 3.5 hours on average in one series and about 245 minutes in the other, with intraoperative complications such as fundus tear and bleeding, and two patients had postoperative dysphagia requiring pneumatic dilatation.

question: Does desflurane alter left ventricular function when used to control surgical stimulation during aortic surgery?
answer: In patients having vascular surgery, desflurane controlled incision-related hypertension in all 16 who developed it, with no change in left ventricular function indices such as fractional area change, circumferential fiber shortening, cardiac index, stroke volume or end-diastolic and end-systolic areas. question: Does loss of consciousness predict neuropsychological decrements after concussion?
answer: In a retrospective study of 383 head-injured patients, those with loss of consciousness did not perform worse on neuropsychological tests than patients with no or uncertain LOC, and no significant group differences were found on any measure. In a study of MTBI patients with and without persistent postconcussion symptoms, loss of consciousness was not predictive of sustained PCS. Poorer cognitive performance was tied to PCS symptom severity rather than to LOC. In elite soccer players, deficits in reaction time after head impacts appeared even in asymptomatic players, and only 6 of the tested cases involved LOC. This suggests neuropsychological changes can occur without LOC.

question: Is the international normalised ratio (INR) reliable?
answer: INR reliability appears conditional: general practice INR results correlated strongly with a reference hospital laboratory using the same method (r=0.96), but correlation fell to 0.86-0.92 against other standard laboratory techniques, and up to 53% of tests could have led to a clinically significant warfarin dose change depending on site and method. Practice-derived INR results showed a positive bias of 0.28 to 1.55 relative to hospital laboratory values, depending on the site and method of testing. In patients sampled the morning after cardiac surgery, INR values were statistically similar from arterial line and peripheral venous samples, whereas APTT ratio differed because of heparin contamination.

question: Blunt trauma in intoxicated patients: is computed tomography of the abdomen always necessary?
answer: Abdominal CT does not appear to be necessary in every intoxicated blunt trauma patient: among 324 patients with blood alcohol ≥80 mg/dL, GCS 15 and an unremarkable abdominal exam, 98% had negative abdominal CT, and only 7 (2%) had abdominal injuries, with 2 (0.6%) needing exploration. question: Can p53 alterations be used to predict tumour response to pre-operative chemo-radiotherapy in locally advanced rectal cancer?
answer: In a study of 48 rectal cancer patients, p53 alterations in pre-treatment biopsies did not significantly predict response to pre-operative chemo-radiation. Tumour size reduction was 53% with wild-type p53 and 63% with altered p53 (P=0.18), and there was no significant difference in local failure. A retrospective study of 81 patients found that low p53 expression, along with high VEGF, p21 and Ki67 expression, correlated with pathologic complete response to pre-operative chemoradiotherapy. A 4-marker score including p53 gave 96.3% sensitivity and 46.3% specificity for pCR. The two directly relevant studies point in different directions: one found no predictive value for p53 alone, while the other found p53 expression correlated with pCR only as part of a multi-marker panel.

question: A short stay or 23-hour ward in a general and academic children's hospital: are they effective?
answer: In a descriptive comparison of short stay wards at a general teaching hospital (Westmead) and an academic children's hospital (New Children's Hospital), the wards appeared effective: they accounted for 10.3% and 14.7% of admissions, with average stays of 17.5 and 20.5 hours and stays over 23 hours in only 1% of admissions. Few short stay admissions needed an in-hospital bed (4% at Westmead vs 6% at New Children's Hospital), and unscheduled returns within 72 hours were under 1%. No adverse events were reported at either short stay ward, parental satisfaction was high, and estimated savings from more efficient bed use were $0.5 million (Westmead) to $2.3 million (New Children's Hospital).

question: Can APC mutation analysis contribute to therapeutic decisions in familial adenomatous polyposis?
answer: APC mutation site correlates with the severity of the natural course of FAP: patients with mutations at codon 1309 were diagnosed about 10 years earlier (mean age 20 years) than those with mutations between codons 168 and 1580 excluding 1309 (mean age 30 years), while mutations at the 5' end of codon 168 or the 3' end of codon 1580 were diagnosed at a mean age of 52 years. question: Is there awareness of pharmaceutical expenditure in the reformed primary care system?
answer: Among 80 primary care doctors in the reformed primary care system in Sabadell, Barcelona, doctors' estimates of their annual pharmaceutical expenditure and of mean prescription cost differed significantly from the real figures, by around twelve million pesetas for annual expenditure, indicating poor awareness of pharmaceutical expenditure. Consistent with this, a survey of British Columbia family physicians found that few estimated costs of common drugs and investigations within 25% of the true cost, with underestimation of expensive items and overestimation of inexpensive drugs. Patient awareness of medication costs was also limited, particularly among pensioners, who knew the cost of only 27% of their prescriptions within 25% error versus 64% for working-age patients.

question: Does transverse apex coincide with coronal apex levels (regional or global) in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis?
answer: The most rotated (transverse apex) vertebral level did not consistently coincide with the coronal apex in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. Compared with the regional and global coronal apexes, it showed higher variability, extending up to two levels for the global apex. The 95% confidence ranges for the difference were -1.19 to +1.54 levels for the global apex and -1.0 to +1.41 levels for the regional apex. By contrast, regional and global coronal apexes were at the same level in 54.5% of curves and within half a level in the other 45.4%, apart from two curves where the regional apex was one level higher.

question: Does the aggressive use of polyvalent antivenin for rattlesnake bites result in serious acute side effects?
answer: In a retrospective review of 65 rattlesnake-bite patients given polyvalent antivenin (mean 12 vials, up to 30), acute side effects occurred in 18% and were almost all urticaria. Only 1 patient (2%) had a serious reaction, requiring a short course of IV epinephrine for blood pressure support, so serious acute side effects were uncommon. The one patient with a serious reaction had a history of a previous antivenin reaction. No other complications occurred, and no deaths, amputations, or permanent disability occurred among antivenin recipients.

question: Does increased nerve length within the treatment volume improve trigeminal neuralgia radiosurgery?
answer: In a randomized trial of 87 patients, irradiating a longer nerve length (two isocenters vs one) did not improve pain relief, which was identical between the two groups. question: Is there still a need for living-related liver transplantation in children?
answer: The one directly relevant study found similar outcomes for split-liver and living-related transplantation. Patient survival was 82% vs 88% and graft survival 76% vs 81%, so split-liver grafts do not clearly replace the need for living-related grafts, nor does the study show living-related transplantation to be clearly superior. question: Is external palliative radiotherapy for gallbladder carcinoma effective?

question: Does rugby headgear prevent concussion?
answer: In a cluster randomized controlled trial of male rugby union teams (under-13 to under-20), padded headgear did not reduce rates of head injury or concussion in the intention-to-treat analysis, with incidence rate ratios of 0.95 and 1.02 for standard headgear versus controls. Analyses based on observed wearing also showed no significant differences, with incidence rate ratios of 1.11 and 1.10 for standard headgear wearers versus nonwearers. In a small questionnaire survey, 62% of players believed headgear could prevent concussion but only 33% of coaches did, which reflects belief rather than evidence of efficacy.

question: Stage I non-small cell lung carcinoma: really an early stage?
answer: After curative resection of stage I NSCLC, overall 5-year survival was 63%, so roughly a third of patients died within 5 years. Survival varied by subgroup: 67% for tumours ≤3 cm versus 46% for tumours >3 cm, and 65% for adenocarcinoma versus 51% for squamous cell carcinoma. Histology, tumour size and a negative resection margin were independent prognostic factors in stage I disease. Survival by T status (66% for T1N0 versus 55% for T2N0) did not differ significantly (P=0.19). Some early-stage patients carry occult adverse features. Positive pre-resectional pleural lavage occurred in 7.3% of stage I patients (3/41), and positive lavage was associated with significantly shorter survival across the whole cohort. In another resection series, women with stage I disease had a significant survival advantage over men (P=0.01). This also indicates that outcomes within stage I are not uniform.

question: Does receipt of hospice care in nursing homes improve the management of pain at the end of life?
answer: Among dying nursing home residents with daily pain, hospice enrollment was associated with better pain management: 51% of hospice residents versus 33% of nonhospice residents received regular analgesic treatment for daily pain (adjusted OR 2.08, 95% CI 1.68-2.56). Fewer hospice residents in daily pain received no analgesics (15% vs 23%; OR 0.57, 95% CI 0.45-0.74) and fewer received analgesics not recommended by AMDA guidelines (21% vs 29%; OR 0.65, 95% CI 0.52-0.80). Morphine derivatives were the most frequently used analgesics among hospice residents (30% of prescriptions), whereas acetaminophen alone was most common among nonhospice residents (25% of prescriptions).

question: Convulsions and retinal haemorrhage: should we look further?
answer: Yes: retinal haemorrhages after a convulsion are uncommon (1 of 153 children in one prospective study; 2 of 182 admitted children in another), so finding them should prompt further investigation, including for child abuse. In the admitted-children study, both children with retinal haemorrhages were eventually diagnosed as abused. In the emergency department study, the one child with haemorrhages after a simple febrile convulsion had no other cause found after thorough investigation, so haemorrhage can occasionally occur after a convulsion without abuse or systemic disease. A case report of a 5-week-old with retinal and intracranial haemorrhage shows that non-abusive causes need to be ruled out, as the cause only became apparent on repeat neuroimaging weeks later.

question: Do lipids, blood pressure, diabetes, and smoking confer equal risk of myocardial infarction in women as in men?
answer: In the Reykjavik cohort, the risk of myocardial infarction or coronary death from these factors was not equal in women and men: systolic blood pressure, ECG-confirmed left ventricular hypertrophy, diabetes or high fasting glucose, triglycerides and smoking were all stronger risk factors in women. Smoking raised risk two- to five-fold in women, increasing with dose, compared with about a doubling in men. Fasting glucose ≥6.7 mmol/L gave an HR of 2.65 in women versus 2.08 in men. Other cohort data support a sex difference for diabetes: in the Renfrew/Paisley cohort, women with diabetes only had a higher adjusted mortality hazard than women with CHD only (HR 1.97), while men showed no significant difference (HR 1.17). Total cholesterol was strongly associated with coronary mortality in both sexes, with similar relative risks for the highest versus lowest fifth (men 3.0, women 3.8).

question: Chemoradiation instead of surgery to treat mid and low rectal tumors: is it safe?
answer: In patients with mid or low rectal tumors who had a clinical complete response after chemoradiation, 8 of 10 had local recurrence within about 4 to 9 months. Only the 2 patients who did not have surgery remained cancer-free, at 37 and 58 months, so omitting surgery does not appear safe. In a UK centre, 6 of 10 patients with T3-4 rectal cancer who had a clinical complete response after chemoradiation and did not undergo surgery developed intrapelvic recurrence, with a median time to local progression of 20 months. Local relapse preceded or coincided with metastatic disease, and no patient underwent salvage resection. Even after chemoradiation plus surgery, outcomes depended on achieving clear margins. Local recurrence was 10% with a negative circumferential resection margin versus 62% with a positive margin, which underscores the importance of resection. Among patients who had chemoradiation followed by total mesorectal excision, 17% of those with a pathological complete response still had involved lymph nodes. This shows that a complete response in the primary tumour does not guarantee node-negative disease.

question: Do mossy fibers release GABA?
answer: Yes: in guinea pig hippocampal slices, stimulating dentate granule cells elicited monosynaptic GABA-A receptor-mediated synaptic signals in CA3 pyramidal neurons, which indicates GABA release by mossy fibers. These inhibitory signals met the criteria that distinguish mossy fiber-CA3 synapses: high sensitivity to metabotropic glutamate-receptor agonists, facilitation during repetitive stimulation, and NMDA receptor-independent long-term potentiation. This physiologic evidence is consistent with the intense GABA and GAD67 immunoreactivity reported in mossy fiber terminals.

question: Are lower fasting plasma glucose levels at diagnosis of type 2 diabetes associated with improved outcomes?
answer: In UKPDS participants, lower fasting plasma glucose at diagnosis was associated with better outcomes: the low FPG group (<7.8 mmol/l) had significantly reduced risk for each predefined clinical outcome except stroke, and the intermediate group had reduced risk for each outcome except stroke and myocardial infarction. Participants with lower FPG at diagnosis less often had retinopathy, abnormal biothesiometer measurements, or reported erectile dysfunction, and the low and intermediate groups had reduced risk of retinopathy progression, reduced vibration sensory threshold, and microalbuminuria development. FPG and HbA1c rose at the same rate in all three diagnosis groups during follow-up, with absolute differences between groups persisting.

question: Increased neutrophil migratory activity after major trauma: a factor in the etiology of acute respiratory distress syndrome?
answer: In a prospective observational study of 17 blunt major trauma patients, neutrophils isolated at admission, 8 h and 24 h migrated significantly more toward high concentrations of interleukin-8 (30 and 100 ng/mL) than neutrophils from normal volunteers, which is consistent with enhanced migration being a factor in the etiology of ARDS. The enhanced migratory response persisted throughout the first 24 hours after injury, whereas neutrophils from normal volunteers showed a physiologic attenuation of migration. Whole-blood neutrophil counts were significantly elevated at admission in patients who later developed ARDS and fell rapidly over the next 24 hours.

question: Is withdrawal-induced anxiety in alcoholism based on beta-endorphin deficiency?
answer: In 60 alcoholics during withdrawal, plasma beta-endorphin was significantly lower than in controls on day 1 and day 14, and was inversely correlated with self-rated anxiety (r=-0.58 on day 1, r=-0.71 on day 14), consistent with an association between beta-endorphin deficiency and withdrawal anxiety. question: Should circumcision be performed in childhood?
answer: In a study of 400 boys aged 0-16, only 11 (2.7%) were considered in need of circumcision, for preputial orifice stenosis (3), a constrictive ring (1), repetitive balanoposthitis (2), or xerosol balanitis (5). A non-retractile foreskin was the most common finding in boys under 1 year (71.5%) and was rare in adolescents (1.6% non-retractile; 82.3% completely retractile), which suggests that retractability develops naturally in most boys. In the same study, 106 boys who had earlier undergone forced dilation had balano-preputial adhesions again, indicating that the prepuce re-adheres in many boys after forced dilation. After EMLA-assisted release of preputial adhesions in 36 symptomatic children, the procedure was successful in 27; 16 of these remained symptom free at 9-12 months, while 11 were listed for circumcision at 2 weeks because of marked recurrence of adhesions.

question: Fragility of the esophageal mucosa: a pathognomonic endoscopic sign of primary eosinophilic esophagitis?
answer: In a series of five patients with dysphagia from histologically confirmed primary eosinophilic esophagitis, all had extremely fragile, inelastic mucosa that tore easily with minor trauma. question: Cue-induced behavioural activation: a novel model of alcohol craving?
answer: In rats trained to self-administer alcohol/saccharin, 5 minutes of exposure to alcohol-associated cues increased active lever responding by 26% and raised blood alcohol levels (8.9 mM vs 7.5 mM), in animals not experiencing withdrawal or relapse, supporting a cue-induced behavioural activation model. The cue effect persisted after a 10-day break from training (29% increase in consumption) and was dose-dependently blocked by naltrexone, consistent with a pharmacologically sensitive craving-like mechanism. The effect was specific to the exposure parameters: 10 or 15 minutes of cues did not change consumption, and 5 minutes in a novel non-alcohol environment decreased responding by 66%. Human data are consistent with cue-triggered drinking behaviour: young adults were more likely to sip alcohol when actors on screen sipped than without such a cue.

question: Can continuous physical training counteract aging effect on myoelectric fatigue?
answer: In 54 physically trained, active skiers aged 24-85, myoelectric fatigue indices of the tibialis anterior did not differ significantly between younger and older subjects, so no correlation between myoelectric fatigue and age was found in physically active people. The study was designed to test whether continuous training can counteract the selective loss of type II muscle fibers seen with aging, and its results are consistent with continuous training counteracting age-related effects on myoelectric fatigue.

question: Spinal subdural hematoma: a sequela of a ruptured intracranial aneurysm?
answer: A single case report describes spinal subdural hematoma arising after subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured internal carotid aneurysm: a 52-year-old woman developed lumbosacral subdural hematoma on postoperative day 6 after craniotomy, so it can occur as a sequela. question: Can patients be anticoagulated after intracerebral hemorrhage?
answer: A decision-analysis model of patients with prior intracerebral hemorrhage and nonvalvular atrial fibrillation favored withholding warfarin, with a gain of 1.9 QALYs for prior lobar ICH and 0.3 QALYs for prior deep hemispheric ICH. question: Is a 9-month treatment sufficient in tuberculous enterocolitis?
answer: In a prospective randomized trial of 40 patients with tuberculous enterocolitis, a 9-month regimen produced a complete response in all patients, the same as a 15-month regimen, and no recurrence occurred in either group during follow-up. question: Injury and poisoning mortality among young men--are there any common factors amenable to prevention?

question: Is there a favorable subset of patients with prostate cancer who develop oligometastases?
answer: Yes: in a retrospective series of 369 prostate cancer patients treated with external beam radiotherapy, those who developed 5 or fewer metastatic lesions had better survival than those with more than 5 lesions (73% and 36% vs 45% and 18% at 5 and 10 years; p = 0.02). Patients with 5 or fewer lesions also had superior metastasis-free survival (p = 0.01) and a longer interval from initial diagnosis to development of bone metastasis (p = 0.02) than those with more than 5 lesions. Once bone metastasis had been diagnosed, survival and the interval from bone metastasis diagnosis to death did not differ significantly between the two groups (p = 0.17 and 0.27). Metastatic site also appeared to matter: patients with bone metastases to the pelvis fared worse than those with vertebral metastases.

question: Is half-dose contrast-enhanced three-dimensional MR angiography sufficient for the abdominal aorta and pelvis?
answer: In a randomized study of 72 patients, overall image quality of abdominal aorta and iliac MR angiography did not differ significantly across four groups that varied in gadolinium concentration, total dose (single vs half) and injection rate, suggesting half-dose imaging can be sufficient. question: Is pain a clinically relevant problem in general adult psychiatry?
answer: In a cross-sectional study of 106 general adult psychiatry inpatients, pain was highly prevalent: point prevalence about 50%, 6-month prevalence 75.5% and 12-month prevalence 76.5%. Almost 10% of patients reported pain lasting at least 3 months in the past year, and impairment and unfitness for work due to pain were related to specific psychiatric diagnoses. Pain was most frequent in patients with affective disorders, followed by neurotic, stress-related and somatoform disorders and then psychotic disorders; depression (OR=6.05) and number of past psychiatric admissions (OR=3.609) were significant risk factors for pain.

question: Does positron emission tomography change management in primary rectal cancer?
answer: In a prospective study of 46 patients with advanced primary rectal cancer, PET changed management in 8 patients (17%), including cancelled surgery in 6 (13%) and a changed radiotherapy field in 2 (4%). PET changed overall tumor stage in 18 of 46 patients (39%), but surgical management was unchanged in 36 of 46 (78%), even though PET upstaged disease in 3 of 36 and downstaged it in 5 of 36. Where follow-up was available, the PET-induced management changes were judged appropriate in each case.

question: Artefacts in 24-h pharyngeal and oesophageal pH monitoring: is simplification of pH data analysis feasible?
answer: Simplifying analysis by leaving out meal periods agreed best with manually corrected 24-h dual-channel pH data and removed many falsely positive reflux episodes, so simplification appears feasible. Using the fraction of time supine, data with meals left out were fully concordant with manually corrected data, and both detected 79% of patients with gastropharyngeal reflux. Not all simplifications work: also excluding a 2-h postprandial period produced 21%-50% falsely negative tests.

question: Do family physicians know the costs of medical care?
answer: Family physicians generally do not know the costs of medical care: in a British Columbia survey, few doctors estimated the costs of 46 common investigations and therapies within 25% of the true cost, and estimates were highly variable. Errors followed a pattern: physicians underestimated the costs of expensive drugs and laboratory investigations and overestimated the costs of inexpensive drugs. Cost awareness did not correlate with sex, practice location, College certification, faculty appointment, or years in practice, so no physician subgroup was identified as cost-aware. A study of primary care doctors in Sabadell, Spain found significant differences between doctors' estimates and actual annual pharmaceutical expenditure and mean prescription costs.

question: Does radiotherapy around the time of pregnancy for Hodgkin's disease modify the risk of breast cancer?
answer: Yes. In a review of 382 women treated with RT for Hodgkin's disease, those irradiated around the time of pregnancy had a much higher overall incidence of breast cancer (16.0% vs. 2.3%, p = 0.0001) and a higher actuarial rate (15-year rate 32.6% vs. 1.7%). In multivariate analysis, pregnancy around the time of RT was the only variable associated with increased breast cancer risk. The risk was concentrated in women irradiated during pregnancy or within 1 month of it (hazard ratio 22.49; 95% CI 5.56-90.88). Breast cancer was diagnosed earlier in women treated around pregnancy, with a median latency of 13.1 years versus 18.9 years in nonpregnant women.

question: Do acute changes in heart rate by isoproterenol affect aortic stiffness in patients with hypertension?
answer: In 17 hypertensive patients, acute heart rate increases produced by graded isoproterenol infusion did not significantly change aortic stiffness: deltaPWV, deltaC and deltaCi showed no significant differences across deltaHR groups (p>0.05). question: Three-dimensional ultrasound-validated large-core needle biopsy: is it a reliable method for the histological assessment of breast lesions?
answer: 3D ultrasound-validated large-core needle biopsy was highly reliable for histological assessment of breast lesions: a median of two cores per lesion gave 96.9% sensitivity, 100% specificity, 0% false-positive and 3.1% false-negative rates across all lesions. For lesions that were surgically excised, sensitivity was 96.5%, specificity 100%, false-negative rate 3.5%, and the underestimation rate was 3.4%. Using 3D visualization of the needle in the postfiring position to classify each sample as central, marginal or outside the lesion guided whether further samples were needed, which allowed the high accuracy to be reached with few cores. Separate retrospective work on continuous (2D) sonographic guidance of large-core biopsy of palpable lesions found higher sensitivity with guidance (98%) than without ultrasound documentation (79%), which is consistent with image guidance supporting biopsy accuracy.

question: Are WHO/UNAIDS/UNICEF-recommended replacement milks for infants of HIV-infected mothers appropriate in the South African context?
answer: Home-prepared milks provided only 8-60% of several vitamins and minerals compared with commercial formula, and supplied just 11% of minimum linoleic acid and 67% of minimum alpha-linolenic acid requirements. Replacement feeding was costly and time-consuming: home-prepared milk cost about 20% of average monthly income and commercial formula about 32%, with 21-35 minutes needed to prepare a 120 ml feed.

question: Prostate-specific antigen and free prostate-specific antigen in the early detection of prostate cancer: do combination tests improve detection?
answer: In stored pre-diagnosis serum from the Physicians' Health Study (429 cases, 1,640 controls), combination tests of total and percent free PSA found tests with higher sensitivity and specificity than PSA>4.0 ng/mL in 29 of 35 train-test splits, and all of them extended the PSA reflex range below 4.0 ng/mL. question: Alcohol consumption and acute myocardial infarction: a benefit of alcohol consumed with meals?

question: Does reducing spasticity translate into functional benefit?
answer: A pooled analysis of two randomized botulinum toxin trials in stroke found a significant relationship between the maximum reduction in arm spasticity and the maximum improvement in arm function (rho = -0.2822, p = 0.0008, n = 137). The spasticity-function relationship was clearer in patients given Dysport at 500 or 1000 units (rho = -0.5679 and -0.4430), but was not seen with placebo or 1500 units. In a placebo-controlled trial in long term care patients with severe upper limb spasticity, botulinum toxin A reduced spasticity and improved passive range of movement. It also lowered caregiver burden (60% vs 8% with a significant reduction at week 6) and improved goal attainment, with effects lasting to week 24. In post-stroke shoulder spasticity, botulinum toxin A did not reduce pain more than placebo. It did improve the hygiene disability score at week 4, with a trend toward improved dressing (p = 0.061).

question: Is the clinically positive axilla in breast cancer really a contraindication to sentinel lymph node biopsy?
answer: The evidence suggests a clinically positive axilla is not necessarily a contraindication to SLN biopsy: in 106 patients with palpable suspicious nodes undergoing SLN biopsy, clinical examination was inaccurate in 41% and falsely positive in 53% of moderately suspicious and 23% of highly suspicious cases. question: Does increased use of private health care reduce the demand for NHS care?
answer: In a prospective survey of GP referrals from 10 UK practices, NHS referral rates were higher, not lower, in wards with high private referral rates (rate ratio 1.40, 95% CI 1.15 to 1.71) after adjusting for deprivation and practice, which does not support the idea that greater private use reduces NHS demand. question: Is coeliac disease screening in risk groups justified?
answer: In a long-term follow-up (median 14 years) of 53 screen-detected coeliac patients from risk groups, 96% adhered to a strict or fairly strict gluten-free diet, and their quality of life and gastrointestinal symptoms were similar to symptom-detected patients and non-coeliac controls, with bone mineral density similar to the general population. question: Is grandmultiparity an independent risk factor for adverse perinatal outcomes?
answer: In a California cohort of 25,512 grandmultiparous and 265,060 multiparous women aged 30 or older, grandmultiparity remained associated with higher adjusted odds of several adverse outcomes, including neonatal death (OR 1.5), preterm delivery (OR 1.3), abruptio placentae (OR 1.3) and fetal macrosomia (OR 1.5). question: Percutaneous ethanol injection for benign cystic thyroid nodules: is aspiration of ethanol-mixed fluid advantageous?

question: Does a well developed collateral circulation predispose to restenosis after percutaneous coronary intervention?
answer: In a prospective study of 58 patients undergoing elective single-vessel PCI, a well developed collateral circulation did not predispose to in-stent restenosis at six months. Restenosis rates were similar in the poor and good collateral groups (diameter 35% vs 43%, p=0.76; area 27% vs 45%, p=0.34; volumetric 23% vs 24%, p=0.84). Collateral flow index was not correlated with diameter, area, or volumetric restenosis (r2<0.1 for each). Stent diameter, stent length, >10% residual stenosis, and smoking history were predictive of restenosis instead.

question: Is high-sensitivity C-reactive protein associated with carotid atherosclerosis in healthy Koreans?

question: Transgastric endoscopic splenectomy: is it possible?

question: Dose end-tidal carbon dioxide measurement correlate with arterial carbon dioxide in extremely low birth weight infants in the first week of life?
answer: In ventilated ELBW infants in the first week of life, EtCO2 correlated well with PaCO2, with an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.81 across 754 paired measurements from 31 infants. Agreement was imperfect: EtCO2 was systematically lower than PaCO2, with an overall bias of 5.6 ± 6.9 mmHg (95% CI 5.11-6.09), and EtCO2 exceeded PaCO2 in only 11.8% of pairs. Using an EtCO2 range of 30 to 50 mmHg, capnography identified 84% of instances where PaCO2 was between 35 and 55 mmHg.

question: Does the severity of obstructive sleep apnea predict patients requiring high continuous positive airway pressure?
answer: In 353 OSA patients with successful manual CPAP titration, OSA severity predicted the need for high CPAP (≥12 cm H2O): high CPAP was required in 28.6% of severe OSA patients versus 6.9% of mild and 5.8% of moderate, and severe OSA was associated with 5.90-fold more frequent high CPAP use after adjustment (95% CI 2.67-13.1). Mean optimal CPAP rose with OSA severity, from 7.79 cm H2O in mild to 8.7 in moderate and 10.1 in severe OSA, and AHI was significantly higher in patients needing high CPAP on univariate analysis. In a small obese cohort, the 95th centile autoCPAP pressure showed a moderate correlation with OSA severity (AHI r = 0.34; ODI r = 0.48), though not with BMI, neck circumference or waist circumference.

question: Can decisional algorithms replace global introspection in the individual causality assessment of spontaneously reported ADRs?
answer: Decisional algorithms do not appear able to replace global introspection: in 500 adverse reports, 15 published algorithms showed high sensitivity (average 93%) but very low specificity (average 7%) compared with the WHO global introspection method. The algorithms' average positive predictive value was 89% and negative predictive value 31%, so they classified nearly all reports as at least possibly drug related and were poor at identifying non-drug-related reports.

question: Do all ethnic groups in New Zealand exhibit socio-economic mortality gradients?
answer: All four New Zealand ethnic groups studied (Asian, Pacific, Maori and European) showed deprivation gradients in all-cause mortality (life expectancy) for 1999-2003, by NZDep2001 quintile and sex. question: Volume change of uterine myomas during pregnancy: do myomas really grow?
answer: Myomas generally do not grow during pregnancy: in a study of 107 pregnant women, most myomas decreased in volume, with 55.1% shrinking between the first and second study periods (mean decrease 35%) and 75% shrinking between the second and third (mean decrease 30%). A substantial minority of myomas did enlarge, 44.9% in the first-to-second interval (mean increase 69%) and 25% in the second-to-third interval (mean increase 102%), so growth occurs in some women but is not the typical pattern.

question: Is a patient's self-reported health-related quality of life a prognostic factor for survival in non-small-cell lung cancer patients?
answer: In 391 advanced NSCLC patients, pretreatment self-reported HRQOL scores for pain and dysphagia were independent prognostic factors for survival in multivariate Cox analysis (pain HR 1.11 and dysphagia HR 1.12 per 10-point worsening, both significant), alongside gender and performance status. In a 206-patient advanced NSCLC trial cohort, several EORTC subscales (pain, appetite loss, fatigue, lung cancer symptoms, overall QOL, physical functioning) predicted poorer survival in univariate analysis. After adjustment for clinical factors, overall QOL was not a significant predictor in that cohort, but the pain subscale remained prognostic (a 40-point increase was associated with a 27% higher hazard).

question: Does Paget's disease exist in India?
answer: Paget's disease of bone does exist in India: a case series documented 21 patients with the disease, with a mean age at presentation of 49.2 years and a male to female ratio of 2.5:1. Of the 21 patients, 15 (71.4%) had polyostotic and 6 (28.6%) had monoostotic disease, most commonly involving the skull and spine (61.9%), pelvis (38.1%) and femur (33.3%). Presentations included bone pain, fracture, deafness, hydrocephalus and paraparesis. Mean serum alkaline phosphatase fell from 1514 IU/L at diagnosis to 454 IU/L nine months after bisphosphonate treatment (P<0.03).

question: Do mutations causing low HDL-C promote increased carotid intima-media thickness?
answer: In a case-control study of carriers of 10 different LCAT, ABCA1 and APOA1 mutations, carotid intima-media thickness was nearly identical in cases (0.66±0.17) and controls (0.65±0.18) despite markedly lower HDL cholesterol (0.67 vs. 1.58 mmol/l) and apolipoprotein A-I in cases. This suggests that low HDL-C caused by these genetic mutations does not promote increased carotid intima-media thickness, in contrast to the inverse HDL–CHD relationship seen in observational data.

question: Cigarettes and cinema: does parental restriction of R-rated movie viewing reduce adolescent smoking susceptibility?
answer: In a survey of 1687 Wisconsin middle school students, greater parental restriction of R-rated movie viewing was associated with lower smoking susceptibility (r = -.36, p<.001). Compared with full restriction, partial restriction (OR 2.1, 95% CI 1.5-2.8) and no restriction (OR 3.3, 95% CI 2.3-4.6) were associated with higher odds of susceptibility, after controlling for demographics and family and friend smoking. Results were similar when smoking prevalence was the outcome: partial restriction had an OR of 1.5 (95% CI 1.0-2.2) and no restriction an OR of 2.5 (95% CI 1.7-3.7) relative to full restriction.

question: Acute hepatitis C in Israel: a predominantly iatrogenic disease?
answer: In a retrospective chart review at three Israeli liver clinics, iatrogenic transmission was the most frequent route of infection (65%) among 29 patients with acute hepatitis C, which supports a predominantly iatrogenic pattern. The iatrogenic transmissions involved several, often minimal, procedures across various clinical settings. Injecting drug use was the second most common route. Patients in the suspected iatrogenic group were older and more often in monogamous relationships than patients in other transmission groups. Spontaneous seroconversion occurred in about one third of patients.

question: Is size-reducing ascending aortoplasty with external reinforcement an option in modern aortic surgery?
answer: In a retrospective series of 50 patients, size-reducing ascending aortoplasty with external non-coated Dacron reinforcement had low hospital mortality (2%) and low morbidity, significantly reduced aortic diameter (CT 55.8 to 40.5 mm; echo 54.1 to 38.7 mm), and remained stable over a mean 70 months of follow-up. The procedure was mostly performed together with other operations, such as aortic valve replacement (47 of 50 patients), subvalvular myectomy (29) and CABG (13), so it can be used as an adjunct in combined cardiac surgery. In adults with conotruncal anomalies, no ascending aortic reoperations followed prior reduction aortoplasty or supracoronary grafts, and no late aortic dissections occurred, with 9 patients having combined aortic valve replacement and reduction aortoplasty.

question: Recurrent spontaneous abortion and skewed X-inactivation: is there an association?
answer: In a sample of 357 women with recurrent spontaneous abortion, the rate of extreme X-inactivation skewing (90% or greater) was 8.6%, which did not differ statistically from the infertility, spontaneous abortion, or multiparous control groups, so no association with recurrent loss was found. The only group that differed significantly was the primiparous group, with 1.0% extreme skewing (P<.01). Skewing rates did not differ between women with at least one live birth (9.9%) and those with no live births and at least 3 losses (5.6%). Women with extreme skewing were on average about 2 years older than those without it (P<.05).

question: Does menopausal transition affect the quality of life?
answer: In a 2-year cohort of 579 premenopausal women in Kinmen, the menopausal transition did not influence any of the eight SF-36 quality-of-life domains in multivariate regression. Vasomotor symptoms, rather than menopausal transition itself, adversely influenced the role limitation due to emotional problems domain, and vitality declined whether women stayed premenopausal or entered perimenopause.

question: Is the holmium:YAG laser the best intracorporeal lithotripter for the ureter?
answer: No supplied study compares holmium:YAG laser head-to-head with other intracorporeal lithotripters, so whether it is the best cannot be determined. A single-arm series of 208 ureteral stones reported 92.7% success at ureteroscopy and 96.7% at 3 months with holmium laser, with no perforations and one stricture. For comparison, a retrospective series of pneumatic lithotripsy for ureteral stones larger than 10 mm reported an 85.2% stone-free rate and 92.3% fragmentation rate. Complications included migration (7.1%), urosepsis (4.5%) and perforation (1.3%).

question: Is renal warm ischemia over 30 minutes during laparoscopic partial nephrectomy possible?
answer: Yes: in a series of 18 patients who underwent laparoscopic partial nephrectomy with warm ischemia over 30 minutes, kidney damage markers and renal function markers had returned to the normal range at 1 year, and GFR at 3 months did not differ significantly from baseline. Scintigraphy of the operated kidney showed a reduction in its function share, from 48.35% before surgery to 36.88% on day 5, 40.56% at 3 months, and 42.8% at 1 year, with all postoperative values still significantly different from baseline. A canine model supports the tolerability of prolonged warm ischemia: after 90 minutes of renal artery occlusion, solitary kidneys regained basal function from week 2, and kidneys in dogs with two kidneys recovered from week 3 with a 23% clearance reduction at 4 weeks.

question: Does normothermic normokalemic simultaneous antegrade/retrograde perfusion improve myocardial oxygenation and energy metabolism for hypertrophied hearts?
answer: In hypertrophied pig hearts, normothermic normokalemic simultaneous antegrade/retrograde perfusion (NNSP) did not improve myocardial oxygenation or energy metabolism relative to antegrade perfusion (NNAP). At full LAD flow both maintained normal levels, and at reduced flow NNSP was equal or worse. At 50% of control LAD flow, NNSP caused a small but significant decrease in myocardial oxygenation and phosphocreatine, whereas NNAP produced no significant change. At 20% of control LAD flow, both techniques substantially decreased oxygenation, ATP and phosphocreatine and increased inorganic phosphate, with significantly greater changes during NNSP than NNAP.

question: Doppler examination of uteroplacental circulation in early pregnancy: can it predict adverse outcome?
answer: In a study of 105 women scanned at 6-12 weeks, those who later had an adverse pregnancy outcome (n=16) had significantly higher right uterine artery PI and RI than women with normal outcomes, so early Doppler of the uteroplacental circulation was associated with adverse outcome. Spiral artery PI and RI were also higher in the adverse-outcome group, but the difference was not statistically significant. Uterine artery Doppler at 20 weeks (mean RI above the 90th percentile plus bilateral diastolic notches) predicted later complications with a positive predictive value of 57% for severe complications and 93% for any complications; later scans at 28 and 36 weeks were less useful.

question: Are sugars-free medicines more erosive than sugars-containing medicines?
answer: In an in vitro study of 97 paediatric medicines, sugars-free formulations were not significantly more erosive than sugars-containing ones: mean pH was 5.73 vs 5.26 and titratable acidity 0.413 vs 0.139 mmol, with no significant difference (P>0.05). question: Do hospitals provide lower quality care on weekends?
answer: In a large Medicare cohort of AMI patients, weekend admission was linked to significantly less immediate intensive cardiac procedures (3.47-point lower catheterization at 1 day, 1.52-point lower angioplasty, 0.35-point lower bypass surgery) and worse outcomes, suggesting lower quality care on weekends for this condition. Weekend AMI patients had a 0.38 percentage point higher 1-year mortality and a 0.20 point higher 1-year readmission with congestive heart failure; the main effect appeared to be delayed treatment, as weekend-weekday procedure gaps narrowed over time.

question: Is fetal anatomic assessment on follow-up antepartum sonograms clinically useful?
answer: In a retrospective study of women with a prior normal anatomic survey, full anatomic assessment on follow-up sonograms detected unanticipated fetal anomalies in 21 of 294 women (7.1%), most often renal pyelectasis. Yield was higher when follow-up sonography was done for fetal growth evaluation than for other indications (12.3% vs 3.5%, P = .01). Neonates of mothers scanned for growth had a higher rate of neonatal intervention (surgical or medical therapy or arranged subspecialty follow-up) than those in the non-growth group (6 of 15 [40.0%] vs 0 of 6, P = .04), suggesting that detected anomalies had clinical consequences.

question: Can computerised tomography replace bone scintigraphy in detecting bone metastases from breast cancer?
answer: In a prospective comparison of 77 CT (thorax, abdomen, pelvis) and bone scan pairs in newly diagnosed metastatic breast cancer, CT detected bone metastases in 43 of 44 patients (98%), suggesting CT including the pelvis can largely replace bone scintigraphy. The single patient missed by CT had a solitary, asymptomatic bony metastasis in the femoral shaft, whereas bone scan was positive in all patients with bone metastases. Bone scintigraphy produced 11 false positive findings, a drawback not reported for CT in this study.

question: Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme and frequency of severe hypoglycaemia in Type 1 diabetes: does a relationship exist?
answer: In 300 people with Type 1 diabetes, serum ACE showed a statistically significant but very weak association with severe hypoglycaemia incidence (Spearman r = 0.115, P = 0.047). question: Suturing of the nasal septum after septoplasty, is it an effective alternative to nasal packing?
answer: In a randomized prospective study of 169 septoplasty patients, septal suturing performed comparably to nasal packing: minor early oozing occurred in 15.3% (suture) vs 13% (packing), and residual septal deviation was the same (5.9%) in both groups. Suturing was associated with fewer complications than packing in the same study: bleeding after pack removal, septal hematoma (4.8% each) and septal perforation (2.4%) were reported only in the packing group, and postoperative adhesions were less frequent with suturing (1.1% vs 5.9%). The cost of suturing was a modestly longer operating time, about 4 minutes more than with packing.

question: Does HER2 immunoreactivity provide prognostic information in locally advanced urothelial carcinoma patients receiving adjuvant M-VEC chemotherapy?
answer: In locally advanced urothelial carcinoma patients receiving adjuvant M-VEC, HER2 immunoreactivity was a significant prognostic factor for progression-free survival (p=0.03) and disease-specific overall survival (p=0.02) in univariate analysis. Across the whole cohort of advanced urothelial carcinoma patients (surgery alone or adjuvant M-VEC), HER2 immunoreactivity was significantly associated with PFS (p=0.02) and disease-specific OS (p=0.005), and was more frequent in bladder than upper urinary tract tumours (60.7% vs 20.7%).

question: Are pectins involved in cold acclimation and de-acclimation of winter oil-seed rape plants?

question: Differentiation of nonalcoholic from alcoholic steatohepatitis: are routine laboratory markers useful?
answer: In a biopsy-based series of 95 steatohepatitis patients, routine laboratory parameters helped distinguish NASH from ASH: MCV, AST/ALT ratio and sex were independent regressors, giving a combined model with aROC 0.92. MCV was elevated in 53% of ASH patients but normal in all NASH patients (P<0.0001), and an AST/ALT ratio >1 was more common in ASH (54.1% vs 20.7%). High-grade fibrosis was more frequent in ASH (59% vs 19%), and the AST/ALT ratio and age independently predicted high-grade fibrosis; MCV differences were more marked in high-grade fibrosis.

question: Biomechanical and wound healing characteristics of corneas after excimer laser keratorefractive surgery: is there a difference between advanced surface ablation and sub-Bowman's keratomileusis?
answer: Yes, the study suggests differences: in a histologic, ultrastructural and tensile-strength study of human corneas, PRK and advanced surface ablation (ASA), and secondarily sub-Bowman's keratomileusis (SBK), were suggested to be biomechanically safer than conventional LASIK regarding risk of post-surgical keratectasia. The study found the stronger, more rigid regions of the cornea were located anteriorly and peripherally, which supported its morphologic findings on collagen fibril direction and lamellar interweaving. Wound healing differs by technique: ASA cases can still develop corneal haze or breakthrough haze from hypercellular fibrotic stromal scarring, whereas SBK, like conventional LASIK, retains short- and long-term potential for interface wound complications from a hypocellular primitive stromal scar. Both approaches share a limitation of inadequate reparative healing, since adult human corneal stromal wounds heal slowly and incompletely.

question: Does confined placental mosaicism account for adverse perinatal outcomes in IVF pregnancies?
answer: A retrospective Dutch CVS study did not find that confined placental mosaicism is more common after IVF/ICSI: incidence was lower in IVF/ICSI pregnancies than in spontaneous conceptions (1.3% vs 2.2%, OR 0.59, 95% CI 0.19-1.85), and the difference was not statistically significant. question: Are wandering and physically nonaggressive agitation equivalent?
answer: Wandering and physically nonaggressive agitation (PNA) were not equivalent concepts: in 181 ambulatory residents with dementia, wandering correlated strongly with PNA Factor 1 (r = 0.68) but only weakly with PNA Factor 2 (r = 0.26). question: The promise of specialty pharmaceuticals: are they worth the price?
answer: The one record that addresses specialty pharmaceuticals directly says they promise longer life expectancy, better quality of life, higher productivity and lower disease burden, but at significant cost and with a need for special handling and distribution; it holds that costs can be controlled with pharmacoeconomic models that assess value. Worth depends on the drug, the population and the price. A modeled knee osteoarthritis preventive drug was cost-effective only for a high-risk cohort (ICER about $118,000 per QALY), and prices of $3,000 per year or more exceeded cost-effectiveness thresholds. Flutamide for metastatic prostate cancer was estimated at about $18,000-$53,700 per QALY saved, depending on the disease severity and the trial data used. Atypical antipsychotics for treatment-resistant depression raised pharmacy and mental-health costs compared with other second-line options, with no difference in total healthcare costs, hospitalizations or ED visits.

answer: In a study of a web-based diabetes information system, none of the general practice structural characteristics (list size, training status, number of GPs, GP age, female GPs, deprivation) were associated with online use, except the number of diabetes-educated staff, which was consistently associated with higher use by nurses and GPs. question: Does a physician's specialty influence the recording of medication history in patients' case notes?
answer: Yes. In a cross-sectional review of 900 patient records across nine specialties at a Nigerian teaching hospital, physician specialty significantly influenced both the depth and the frequency of medication history documentation (P<0.0001). question: Do older patients who refuse to participate in a self-management intervention in the Netherlands differ from older patients who agree to participate?
answer: Yes. question: Can homemade alcohol (Raksi) be useful for preserving dead bodies?
answer: In sacrificed rats, intraventricular Raksi (about 34% alcohol) arrested postmortem changes for up to 72 hours, whereas distilled-water controls showed moderate to severe postmortem changes. Mild putrefactive changes, gas liberation and tissue liquefaction appeared in the Raksi group only at 96 hours, so the authors concluded Raksi can be used temporarily for embalming, as an alternative when standard embalming constituents are unavailable.

question: Do the changes in the serum levels of IL-2, IL-4, TNFalpha, and IL-6 reflect the inflammatory activity in the patients with post-ERCP pancreatitis?
answer: In 45 patients undergoing therapeutic ERCP, early serum cytokine changes differed between the 7 who developed post-ERCP pancreatitis and those who did not, which supports these changes reflecting inflammatory activity in post-ERCP pancreatitis. question: Is the histidine triad nucleotide-binding protein 1 (HINT1) gene a candidate for schizophrenia?
answer: Evidence on HINT1 is mixed: an Irish study found nominally significant allele-frequency differences at several SNPs, but only in sex-stratified analyses, and the sex effect differed between the two samples. Brain expression did not differ significantly between patients and controls. HINT1 lies on chromosome 5q31.2, a region implicated in schizophrenia linkage studies. It has previously been reported to be differentially expressed in postmortem brain and linked to dysregulated postsynaptic dopamine transmission, which supports its status as a candidate gene. A significant interaction among sex, diagnosis and rs3864283 genotype was observed in the expression data. This suggests a possible sex-dependent role for HINT1 variation.

question: The FOOTSTEP self-management foot care programme: are rheumatoid arthritis patients physically able to participate?
answer: In a cohort of 30 RA patients, only 57% passed all the physical tests (sight, reach, grip) needed for self-managed foot care under FOOTSTEP, so many but not all were physically able to participate. question: Therapeutic anticoagulation in the trauma patient: is it safe?
answer: In a retrospective review of 114 trauma patients on therapeutic heparin, 21% had at least one anticoagulation complication (most often a hemoglobin drop requiring transfusion) and 4% died, 3 of those deaths with significant hemorrhage attributed to anticoagulation. This suggests therapeutic anticoagulation in trauma carries a substantial risk of complications rather than being uniformly safe. Complications were associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (OR 9.2), unfractionated heparin use versus fractionated heparin (OR 3.8), and lower initial platelet count, so risk varied by patient and treatment characteristics. In blunt traumatic intracranial hemorrhage, patients given LMWH (prophylactic chemoprophylaxis) had more hemorrhage progression than those not given it (42% vs 24%), and 4.1% of LMWH patients needed neurosurgical intervention for progression. This indicates heightened bleeding concern in the head-injured subgroup, though the dose was prophylactic rather than therapeutic.

question: Can we predict which head and neck cancer survivors develop fears of recurrence?
answer: In a prospective study of 82 head and neck cancer patients, fear of cancer recurrence after treatment was directly predicted by pre-treatment fear of recurrence and by optimism, so some prediction is possible. question: Is motion perception deficit in schizophrenia a consequence of eye-tracking abnormality?
answer: The direct evidence is mixed: speed discrimination thresholds did not differ between patients (n=38) and controls (n=33) at 150 msec, when eye tracking was unlikely, but patients had significantly higher thresholds at 300 msec, when eye movements could intrude. This suggests the motion perception deficit appears under conditions that allow eye tracking, but it does not show that it is simply a consequence of eye-tracking abnormality. Eye-tracking frequency during the 300 msec stimulus correlated with speed discrimination in controls but not in patients, suggesting that eye-tracking initiation may help controls but not patients.

question: Is there a discrepancy between patient and physician quality of life assessment?
answer: Yes, in a urogynecology clinic, physician and patient KHQ quality-of-life assessments showed relatively poor concordance (mean weighted kappa 0.33, range 0.18-0.57), with physicians underestimating the impact of LUTS on social limitations and emotions (P<0.05). Physician scores deviated in both directions: they underestimated QoL score in 4 of 9 domains (mean 5.5%) and overestimated it in 5 of 9 domains (mean 6.9%). In Crohn's disease, physicians perceived a lower disease burden (median 12.5) than patients reported (median 20), although patient and physician perception of current health correlated well (0.73). Among adolescents, parent-proxy HRQL scores (global and dimension scores) differed significantly from the adolescents' own scores, which is a related patient-versus-observer discrepancy but not a physician comparison.

question: Is the zeolite hemostatic agent beneficial in reducing blood loss during arterial injury?
answer: In a swine femoral artery injury model, applying the zeolite agent QuikClot decreased total blood loss compared with pressure dressing over gauze. question: Do emergency medical services professionals think they should participate in disease prevention?
answer: In a survey of 27,233 EMS professionals, 82.7% (99% CI 82.1-83.3) felt that EMS professionals should participate in disease prevention. Support was lowest among those working 20 to 29 hours per week (67.4%), and was higher among respondents who had participated in prevention programs (92% vs. 82%). Support was weaker for delivering prevention during emergency calls: about half (51.1%) agreed it should be provided then, and only 7.7% reported doing so. Among those who had done so, 81% thought it should be provided during emergency calls.

question: Does the enteral feeding advancement affect short-term outcomes in very low birth weight infants?
answer: In a prospective study of 1430 VLBW infants in 13 German centers, slow advancement to full enteral feeds was associated with significantly more late-onset sepsis than rapid advancement (20.4% vs 14.0%; P=0.002), along with more central venous line use (48.6% vs 31.1%) and antibiotic use (92.4% vs 77.7%). question: Gender difference in survival of resected non-small cell lung cancer: histology-related phenomenon?

question: Does ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament affect the neurological outcome after traumatic cervical cord injury?
answer: In 129 patients with nonsurgically treated acute C3-C4 cervical spinal cord injury, OPLL at the injury site (13 patients) was not associated with significantly different ASIA motor scores at admission or discharge compared with patients without OPLL. question: Very high serum CA 19-9 levels: a contraindication to pancreaticoduodenectomy?
answer: Very high preoperative CA 19-9 (≥900 IU/ml) did not worsen survival compared with high levels (400-899 IU/ml) after pancreatoduodenectomy, so very high levels alone do not appear to be a contraindication to resection. question: Is determination between complete and incomplete traumatic spinal cord injury clinically relevant?
answer: Yes: in a prospective multicenter cohort of 432 patients with traumatic SCI, the complete/incomplete distinction was prognostically useful for 1-year independent ambulation (AUC 0.823), but sacral sparing measures combined (voluntary anal contraction plus S4-5 light touch and pin prick) discriminated significantly better (AUC 0.906). question: Surgical treatment of prosthetic valve endocarditis in patients with double prostheses: is single-valve replacement safe?
answer: In 20 patients with PVE and both mitral and aortic prostheses, replacing only the valve that appeared infected (13 patients) was followed by cure without relapse in all 9 who survived surgery and completed antimicrobial therapy, over about 15.8 months of follow-up. question: Does sonographic needle guidance affect the clinical outcome of intraarticular injections?
answer: Sonographic needle guidance improved clinical outcomes of intraarticular injections in a randomized trial of 148 painful joints. Compared with palpation guidance, it reduced procedural pain by 43.0% and 2-week pain scores by 58.5%, and it increased the responder rate by 25.6%. A second randomized trial of effusive knees found the same direction of effect. Ultrasound guidance gave 48% less procedural pain, a 183% larger aspirated synovial fluid volume, and lower VAS pain at 2 weeks (1.5 vs 2.8 cm, p=0.034). Sonography also increased the detection of effusion by 200% and the aspirated fluid volume by 337% in the joint-injection trial.

question: Has the 80-hour workweek improved surgical resident education in New England?
answer: A survey of New England surgical residency programs found no evidence that the 80-hour workweek improved resident education: only 25% of responding programs felt education improved, 31% felt it worsened, and 44% perceived no difference. question: Autoerotic asphyxiation: secret pleasure--lethal outcome?
answer: Autoerotic asphyxiation, in which hypoxia is induced to enhance sexual excitement, is not uncommon among children, preteens, and adolescents and can lead to unintended death. Practitioners can miscalculate the danger of the situation they have contrived and lose their gamble with death; the practice is typically clandestine and elusive, which is why pediatrician awareness and willingness to discuss it may help prevent a tragedy.

question: Should prostate specific antigen be adjusted for body mass index?
answer: In 994 men without prostate cancer in the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, body mass index was not significantly associated with PSA after adjusting for age (p = 0.06), and a 10-point BMI increase corresponded to a negligible PSA difference of -0.03 ng/ml (95% CI -0.40 to 0.49), so the study does not support adjusting PSA for BMI. The null finding was consistent when men with prostate cancer were included, when percent body fat replaced BMI, and after adjusting for prostate volume; longitudinal weight changes were also not significantly associated with PSA.

question: Can the prognosis of polymyalgia rheumatica be predicted at disease onset?

question: Is prophylactic fixation a cost-effective method to prevent a future contralateral fragility hip fracture?
answer: In a Markov cost-effectiveness model, prophylactic fixation of the uninjured hip was not cost-effective in the baseline case of a 79-year-old woman (ICER $142,795/QALY, versus a $50,000/QALY threshold). Cost-effectiveness improved when the additional cost of prophylaxis was under $6000, but in most analyses the result was highly sensitive to the effectiveness of the procedure and to the morbidity and mortality of the additional operation.
