question: Proof of concept study: does fenofibrate have a role in sleep apnoea syndrome?
answer: In a 4-week randomized, double-blind proof-of-concept trial of 34 sleep apnoea patients, fenofibrate 145 mg significantly reduced the percentage of time with SpO2<90% (9.0% to 3.5% vs. 10.0% to 11.5% with placebo, p=0.007). However, the apnoea/hypopnoea index did not change significantly (14% reduction vs. control, 95%CI -47 to 40%, p=0.533), so the effect is only partial. Fenofibrate also reduced obstructive apnoeas (by 44%, p=0.048) and non-cortical micro-awakenings related to respiratory events (23.5 to 18.0 per hour vs. 24.0 to 25.0 with placebo, p=0.004). Other sleep variables were not significantly influenced.

question: Fulfilling human resources development goal in West Africa: can the training of ophthalmologist diplomates be improved?
answer: A 2006 survey of 12 trainee ophthalmologist diplomats in the West African Ophthalmic Diploma Training programme found most were satisfied with it, but they identified problems and suggested changes that could improve training. Trainees reported inadequate sponsorship (33.3%), short course duration (33.3%) and poor accommodation (16.7%) as problems. They suggested more training posts (33.3%), higher training allowances (25.0%) and incentives for trainers and training hospitals (16.7%). Most trainees rated the programme as well structured (75.0%) and rated their own skills at least good in cataract surgery (91.7%), pterygium (83.3%) and trabeculectomy (75.0%). Perceived training allowance adequacy was mixed, with 66.7% calling it adequate and 33.3% inadequate.

question: Continuation of pregnancy after antenatal corticosteroid administration: opportunity for rescue?
answer: In a retrospective cohort of 692 women given antenatal corticosteroids at 24-32 weeks, only 17.9% remained pregnant 1 week after the course and delivered at <34 weeks, which is the group that could potentially benefit from rescue corticosteroids. A rescue opportunity therefore exists, but for a minority of women. Most women did not remain pregnant long after the first course: 46.4% delivered within 1 week and 13.3% within 24 hours, while 35.7% delivered at ≥34 weeks. Women who received corticosteroids for premature preterm rupture of membranes (OR 3.83), with twins (OR 2.90), or before 28 weeks (OR 2.21) were more likely to deliver at <34 weeks, identifying groups more likely to have a rescue opportunity.

question: Delayed diagnosis of anorectal malformations: are current guidelines sufficient?
answer: In a later cohort at a referral institution, the diagnosis of an anorectal malformation was delayed beyond 24 h in 14 of 44 referred infants (32%), and across the study the diagnosis was missed in 12 patients despite neonatal examination, which may indicate that current practice does not reliably ensure timely diagnosis. Delayed diagnosis was not associated with gender, birth weight, prematurity, malformation type or associated anomalies, but was associated with presentation with obstructive symptoms (86% vs 27%), including abdominal distension and delayed passage of meconium or stool.

question: Do symptoms predict COPD in smokers?
answer: In a screened work-related cohort (N=3,955), respiratory symptoms were highly sensitive but poorly specific for airflow obstruction in smokers (sensitivity 92%, specificity 19%, PPV 47%, NPV 75%), so symptoms do not reliably identify COPD. Symptoms were common even in smokers without obstruction: 92% of smokers with airflow obstruction reported symptoms, but so did 76% of smokers with normal spirometry and 86% of smokers with restriction. Symptoms and heavy smoking were associated with airflow obstruction (odds ratios about 1.8–2.6 for individual symptoms; 3.73 for ≥20 pack-years), yet 44% of smokers had obstruction and only 36% of those reported a COPD diagnosis or treatment. In a general-population sample of adults aged 45 and older, the predictive values of symptoms for chronic airflow obstruction were also low, consistent with the smoker-specific findings.

question: The English antibiotic awareness campaigns: did they change the public's knowledge of and attitudes to antibiotic use?
answer: A controlled before-and-after survey found no improvement in public understanding that antibiotics do not help coughs and colds in England or Scotland, and no difference between the two countries after the 2008 English campaigns. Campaign poster recall rose modestly in England (23.7% vs 19.2%), but this was only about 2.3% higher than the increase in Scotland. No improvement in antibiotic use was detected, and respondents were significantly more likely to retain leftover antibiotics.

question: A model of healing of Los Angeles grades C and D reflux oesophagitis: is there an optimal time of acid suppression for maximal healing?

question: Is transurethral catheterisation the ideal method of bladder drainage?
answer: Transurethral catheterisation does not appear to be an ideal method of bladder drainage: in a survey of 50 patients after major open abdominal surgery, satisfaction scores were poor (4.18/10 in men vs 2.75/10 in women) and half of the patients had urinary tract infection symptoms after catheter removal. question: Is it appropriate to implant kidneys from elderly donors in young recipients?
answer: In a matched comparison of 91 transplants from donors over 60 into recipients under 60 versus 91 controls with donors and recipients under 60, patient survival (P=0.642), graft survival (P=0.980) and death-censored graft survival (P=0.747) did not differ over 10 years. Acute rejection, delayed graft function (tubular necrosis), need for dialysis and hospital stay were comparable between elderly-donor and control transplants. Supporting this, a separate single-center study found that expanded criteria donor kidneys (which are older donors) had graft survival and rates of delayed graft function and primary nonfunction comparable to standard criteria donor kidneys.

question: A patient with myelomeningocele: is untethering necessary prior to scoliosis correction?
answer: In a retrospective series of 17 myelomeningocele patients who were radiographically tethered on MRI but had no symptomatic tethered cord, scoliosis fusion without prior untethering produced no new cranial nerve palsy, shunt malfunction, urological change, or upper extremity deficit; one patient had transient lower extremity weakness that resolved within 1 month. The same series achieved a mean Cobb angle correction from 82 to 35 degrees (57%) without untethering, with at least 2 years of follow-up. A prospective series of 11 patients with thoracolumbar myelomeningocele undergoing two-stage anterior and posterior fusion reported no increased neurologic deficit or other major complication over a mean follow-up of about 5 years, with curves corrected from 81 to 31 degrees (35 degrees at final follow-up).

question: Is hypoalbuminemia an independent prognostic factor in patients with gastric cancer?
answer: In a study of gastric cancer patients with pretreatment albumin and CRP measurements, hypoalbuminemia was not an independent prognostic factor: albumin predicted survival on univariate analysis (p<0.001) but lost significance on multivariate analysis. question: Is primary angioplasty an acceptable alternative to thrombolysis?
answer: In a randomized trial of STEMI patients in regional hospitals, transport for primary PCI (with tirofiban) had lower 30-day mortality than on-site thrombolysis (3.49% vs 8.88%, p=0.04). It also had lower reinfarction (1.16% vs 5.92%, p=0.02) and a lower combined death/reinfarction/stroke rate (5.23% vs 15.98%, p=0.001). Hospital stay was shorter in the PCI transport group (9 vs 14 days), and no patients died during transfer. About 10% of patients assigned to thrombolysis alone later needed catheterisation-laboratory PCI. Patient satisfaction with primary angioplasty-based care was high and not significantly different from thrombolysis-based care for overall care (78% vs 71% rating 'excellent', P=0.074). Patients rated speed of treatment higher at angioplasty sites (80% vs 67% 'excellent', P=0.001). Carers rated convenience of visiting lower at angioplasty sites (12% vs 1% 'poor'), but in interviews they accepted this inconvenience given the life-saving nature of the treatment.

question: Validation of the 2009 TNM version in a large multi-institutional cohort of patients treated for renal cell carcinoma: are further improvements needed?
answer: In a 5339-patient multicenter cohort, the 2009 TNM primary tumor classification was an independent predictor of cancer-specific survival, but it showed shortcomings that suggest further improvements are needed: pT2b and pT3a had similar CSS, as did pT3c and pT4, and the pT3a and pT3b stages contained patients with heterogeneous outcomes. The pT1 substratification (pT1a vs pT1b) did not retain an independent predictive role in multivariable analysis in the multicenter cohort. A separate long-term single-cohort study found that T3a defined by perinephric fat invasion was inhomogeneous, mixing small tumors with excellent prognosis and large tumors with poor prognosis. A proposed modified TNM that ignores perinephric fat invasion fit better than the 2002 version (Nagelkerke R2 0.439 vs 0.359).

answer: Discordant TEOAE and AABR outcomes were moderately predictable in a Nigerian newborn screening cohort: antenatal care status, mode of delivery and nursery type predicted discordance among screened infants (c-statistic=0.73). question: Is there a role for fondaparinux in perioperative bridging?
answer: Fondaparinux may have a limited role in perioperative bridging, mainly for patients who cannot receive low-molecular-weight heparin or inpatient IV unfractionated heparin, such as those with a history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia or antithrombin III deficiency. For most patients, it may be optimal to avoid its use before surgery. Its extended half-life of 17-21 hours complicates bridging, especially when to stop it before high-bleeding-risk surgery or surgery with neuraxial anesthesia. Published trials used fondaparinux 2.5 mg daily for VTE prophylaxis in surgical patients, and most avoided preoperative use in patients receiving neuraxial anesthesia. Only three case reports describe its use as a bridge, one at 2.5 mg and two at the full treatment dose of 7.5 mg. Professional anesthesia guidelines conflict on the timing of drug administration relative to neuraxial catheter use, and anticoagulation guidelines give minimal direction on perioperative fondaparinux.

question: Is patient outcome compromised during the initial experience with robot-assisted radical cystectomy?
answer: In 164 consecutive robot-assisted radical cystectomy patients, sequential case number (a proxy for early experience) was not significantly associated with complications, blood loss, positive surgical margins, or overall survival, suggesting outcomes were not compromised during the initial experience. Greater case experience was associated with shorter operative time and higher lymph node yield, so the learning-curve effect appeared in process measures rather than in oncologic or safety outcomes. Survival in that cohort was significantly associated with tumour stage, lymph node metastases, and positive surgical margins, not with case sequence. In a multi-institution database of 496 patients, surgeons' prior robotic prostatectomy experience was associated with operative time, blood loss, and lymph node yield, but not with positive surgical margin status (7.0% overall).

question: Does TDP-43 type confer a distinct pattern of atrophy in frontotemporal lobar degeneration?
answer: In pathologically confirmed FTLD-TDP, voxel-based morphometry showed distinct atrophy patterns by TDP-43 type: type 1 had frontotemporal and parietal atrophy, type 2 predominantly anterior temporal atrophy, and type 3 predominantly posterior frontal atrophy. Within type 1, subjects with a progranulin mutation had significantly more lateral temporal lobe atrophy than those without, and all type 2 subjects were diagnosed with semantic dementia. question: Does preoperative anemia adversely affect colon and rectal surgery outcomes?
answer: In 23,348 elective open and laparoscopic colectomies in the NSQIP database, preoperative anemia independently predicted a worse 30-day composite outcome (MI, stroke, progressive renal insufficiency or death), with odds ratios of 1.83 for severe, 2.19 for moderate and 1.49 for mild anemia versus no anemia. question: Is EQ-5D a valid quality of life instrument in patients with acute coronary syndrome?

question: Assessment of carotid artery stenosis before coronary artery bypass surgery. Is it always necessary?
answer: Routine carotid screening does not appear to be necessary for every patient before coronary artery bypass surgery: in a retrospective series of 205 patients, significant carotid stenosis was far more prevalent in the high-risk group (9.1%) than the low-risk group (1.2%), and all perioperative strokes (5/205) and all carotid interventions (5/205) occurred in the high-risk group. Peripheral vascular disease, carotid bruit and diabetes mellitus were significant risk factors for carotid stenosis, and carotid stenosis was itself a risk factor for perioperative stroke, which supports targeting screening to patients with these risk factors.

question: Preoperative staging of patients with liver metastases of colorectal carcinoma. Does PET/CT really add something to multidetector CT?
answer: PET/CT adds information mainly for extrahepatic disease and local recurrence, but not for intrahepatic staging, where MDCT/MR was more sensitive (89.2% vs 55%) in one prospective study of 97 patients. In another prospective study of 76 patients, contrast-enhanced CT and PET/CT had comparable sensitivity for intrahepatic metastases (95% vs 91%), while PET/CT was better for local recurrence (93% vs 53%) and extrahepatic disease (89% vs 64%). PET/CT findings changed the therapeutic strategy in 21% of patients in one study, and in 17 patients in the other, but in the latter the additional information was correct in only eight cases and wrong in nine.

question: Xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis: a premalignant condition?
answer: In a comparative immunohistochemical study, xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis (XGC) showed little of the molecular alteration seen in gallbladder carcinoma: p53 was positive in 3% of XGC vs 52% of GBC, and PCNA in 11% vs 65%. This argues against a premalignant nature for XGC. XGC resembled chronic cholecystitis and control gallbladders rather than carcinoma: PCNA did not differ significantly among these groups, and beta-catenin remained homogeneously membranous, whereas in GBC it shifted to cytoplasmic and nuclear patterns.

question: Do women with ovaries of polycystic morphology without any other features of PCOS benefit from short-term metformin co-treatment during IVF?
answer: In a double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial of 134 women with ovulatory polycystic ovaries and no clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, metformin co-treatment during IVF did not significantly improve outcomes compared with placebo. Live birth rate was 39.1% with metformin versus 46.2% with placebo (OR 0.75, 95% CI 0.38-1.49), and clinical pregnancy was 42.0% versus 50.8%, so there was no benefit and the point estimates were numerically lower with metformin. Severe OHSS rates did not differ between groups (8.7% with metformin versus 7.7% with placebo), so no reduction in OHSS risk was shown.

question: Do mitochondria play a role in remodelling lace plant leaves during programmed cell death?
answer: Mitochondria appear to play a role in developmentally regulated PCD during lace plant leaf perforation: mitochondrial dynamics (distribution, motility, membrane potential) changed in stages (M1-M4) across cells that will not undergo PCD, and cells in early and late PCD. The gradient of fragmented nuclear DNA seen with TUNEL tracked the mitochondrial stages, linking mitochondrial changes to PCD progression. In vivo treatment with cyclosporine A, used to indirectly probe mitochondrial permeability transition pore formation, produced leaves with significantly fewer perforations than controls and with mitochondrial dynamics resembling those of non-PCD cells.

question: Does solid culture for tuberculosis influence clinical decision making in India?
answer: In a retrospective review at a South Indian tertiary hospital, solid culture on Löwenstein-Jensen medium had little influence on clinical decision making: most treatment decisions were made before results were available, and only 2 patients (1.3%) started treatment based on a positive culture. No culture-negative patients discontinued treatment after results, and 124 (82.7%) culture-positive patients had already started treatment before culture results were available. Drug susceptibility testing from culture led to treatment modification in only 4 patients (3.4%), even though 25.2% of tested positive cultures showed some resistance and 6.7% showed multidrug resistance.

question: Do elderly cancer patients have different care needs compared with younger ones?

question: Does growth hormone replacement therapy reduce mortality in adults with growth hormone deficiency?
answer: In a Dutch nationwide retrospective cohort of GHD adults, those treated with GH did not show reduced mortality: 95 died versus 74.6 expected (SMR 1.27, 95% CI 1.04-1.56), i.e. mortality was higher than in the general population. question: Factors determining the survival of nasopharyngeal carcinoma with lung metastasis alone: does combined modality treatment benefit?
answer: In a retrospective cohort of 246 NPC patients with lung metastasis alone, combined therapy was associated with significantly longer median post-metastasis survival (45.6 vs 23.7 months) and overall survival (73.7 vs 46.2 months) than chemotherapy alone (P<0.001). question: Is the h-index predictive of greater NIH funding success among academic radiologists?
answer: The h-index was associated with having any NIH funding but not with greater funding success. question: Do preoperative statins reduce atrial fibrillation after coronary artery bypass grafting?
answer: In a retrospective cohort of 203 CABG patients, postoperative atrial fibrillation was significantly less frequent with preoperative statin therapy than without it (16% vs 33%, p = 0.005). question: Spleen-preserving distal pancreatectomy with resection of the splenic vessels. Should one rely on the short gastric arteries?
answer: One should not rely on the short gastric arteries after spleen-preserving distal pancreatectomy with splenic vessel resection: cadaveric perfusion, intraoperative Doppler and post-operative CT angiography found no effective short gastric supply to the spleen. Intraoperative color Doppler detected no hilar arterial flow after clamping the splenic and left gastroepiploic arteries, and clamping the short gastric arteries did not change flow parameters. In all cases the gastroepiploic arcade, not the short gastric arteries, was the main arterial pathway feeding the spleen after the procedure.

question: Is there a relationship between complex fractionated atrial electrograms recorded during atrial fibrillation and sinus rhythm fractionation?
answer: In patients with persistent AF, no significant correlation was found between CFAE maps recorded during AF and sinus rhythm fractionation maps (r = 0.2; P = NS), even though each covered roughly a quarter to a third of the left atrial surface (CFAE 25% ± 15%, SRF 29% ± 14%). The distribution of sinus rhythm fractionation did not differ significantly between AF patients and normal controls (P = .74), and SRF regions overlapped with areas of wave-front collision 75% ± 13% of the time, suggesting SRF is related to activation patterns rather than to AF-related CFAE substrate.

question: Does intra-abdominal desmoid disease affect patients with an ileal pouch differently than those with an ileorectal anastomosis?
answer: In a retrospective study of 86 FAP patients with intra-abdominal desmoids (49 restorative proctocolectomy/IPAA, 37 ileorectal anastomosis), the clinical course was similar: overall desmoid complication rates were about 70% in both groups, and treatment patterns were the same. Individual complications did not differ meaningfully between groups: bowel obstruction 32.7% vs 48.6%, fistula 10.2% vs 13.5%, pain 34.7% vs 21.6%, and desmoid-related death 2.0% vs 10.8% for IPAA vs IRA respectively. Surgery for desmoid complications was not significantly different (38.8% IPAA vs 51.4% IRA, P=0.21), and permanent stoma rates were essentially identical (22.4% vs 22.2%).

question: Epidural analgesia for surgical treatment of peritoneal carcinomatosis: a risky technique?
answer: In a retrospective series of 35 patients undergoing cytoreductive surgery with HIPEC, epidural analgesia was not associated with spinal haematoma, meningitis or epidural abscess, suggesting it was not a risky technique in this cohort. Some patients had thrombopenia or prothrombin time below 60% (5 patients, 14%) or leukopenia (2 patients, 6%) before catheter removal, but no thrombopenia or coagulation disorders were recorded on the day of catheter removal.

question: Do instrumental activities of daily living predict dementia at 1- and 2-year follow-up?
answer: In a multicenter prospective memory-clinic cohort, IADL disability added predictive value for dementia beyond age, sex, education, depression and cognitive measures at 1-year (OR 2.20, 95% CI 1.51-3.13) and 2-year follow-up (OR 2.11, 95% CI 1.33-3.33). Participants with baseline IADL disabilities converted to dementia more often (24.4%) than those without (16.7%) (P = .04). In a community cohort (PAQUID), a summed score of dependencies on four IADLs predicted dementia at 3 years, and increasing dependence between baseline and 3 years was associated with higher risk of dementia at 5 years, though baseline IADL score did not predict 5-year incident dementia.

question: Is distance to provider a barrier to care for medicaid patients with breast, colorectal, or lung cancer?

question: Can serum be used for analyzing the EGFR mutation status in patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer?
answer: In 57 patients with advanced NSCLC, EGFR mutation status determined from serum (by PNA-LNA PCR clamp) agreed with tumor-tissue sequencing in 50 of 57 pairs (87.7%), with mutations found in serum of 11 patients versus tumor of 12 patients. question: Does performance in selection processes predict performance as a dental student?
answer: The two dental-student studies point in different directions. At Otago, after controlling for other variables, pre-admission academic average, UMAT scores and interview performance did not predict performance as a dental student. At Aberdeen Dental School, multiple mini-interview (MMI) performance correlated with academic performance (r = 0.180, p = 0.001). The student's first degree was also associated with academic scores (p = 0.001). At Otago, the best predictors of final-year class placement were New Zealand European ethnicity and domestic student status, and second-year class place strongly predicted final-year class place. Other socio-demographic characteristics were not associated with performance.

question: Do elderly patients benefit from surgery in addition to radiotherapy for treatment of metastatic spinal cord compression?
answer: In a matched-pair analysis of elderly (>65 years) patients with metastatic spinal cord compression, adding surgery to radiotherapy did not significantly improve motor function (21% vs 24%, p=0.39), 1-year local control (81% vs 91%, p=0.44), or 1-year survival (46% vs 39%, p=0.71) compared with radiotherapy alone. Subgroup matched-pair analyses showed no significant advantage either: for direct decompressive surgery with stabilization plus radiotherapy, motor improvement was 22% vs 24% (p=0.92) and 1-year survival 54% vs 43% (p=0.30); for laminectomy plus radiotherapy, motor improvement was 20% vs 23% (p=0.06) and 1-year survival 32% vs 32% (p=0.55).

question: Can pictorial warning labels on cigarette packages address smoking-related health disparities?
answer: Pictorial warning label effects partly depend on educational attainment. Didactic text was rated higher than testimonial text among more educated participants, but the difference was weaker or non-significant among less educated participants, so the evidence on addressing disparities is mixed. With text held constant, graphic images of diseased organs were rated as more credible, relevant and impactful than images of human suffering. This suggests label content can be chosen to improve perceived effectiveness. In a small randomized trial of adult smokers, pictorial warnings were associated with higher motivation to quit than written warnings alone, and this effect appeared independent of nicotine dependence and self-affirmation.

question: SPECT study with I-123-Ioflupane (DaTSCAN) in patients with essential tremor. Is there any correlation with Parkinson's disease?
answer: In one DaTSCAN SPECT study, patients with essential tremor largely did not show the putaminal dopaminergic loss seen in Parkinson's disease: visual reads of ET patients matched normal volunteers, while all PD patients had reduced putaminal uptake, so ET and PD were distinguishable. However, semiquantitative analysis found reduced striatal uptake in ET compared with normal volunteers, and one ET patient with an equivocal baseline scan deteriorated at 12 months. In patients with unilateral PD, putaminal uptake was significantly reduced contralateral to the affected side compared with both ET patients and normal volunteers. question: Comparative safety of infliximab and etanercept on the risk of serious infections: does the association vary by patient characteristics?
answer: In a Kaiser Permanente Northern California cohort, the infliximab-versus-etanercept association with serious infections varied by age: in the first 3 months, infliximab had an elevated adjusted HR in patients <65 years (HR 3.01; 95% CI 1.49-6.07) but not in those ≥65 years (HR 0.94; 95% CI 0.41-2.13). The same study found no suggestion that the comparative hazard ratio varied by sex, race/ethnicity, body mass index, or smoking status. Crude serious infection incidence in the first 3 months was higher in patients ≥65 years (16.0 per 100 person-years) than in those <65 years (5.4 per 100 person-years).

question: Does a 4 diagram manual enable laypersons to operate the Laryngeal Mask Supreme®?
answer: In a manikin pilot study, 150 laypersons given a four-illustration instruction sheet mostly operated the Laryngeal Mask Supreme successfully: 96.7% inserted it in the right direction, and 79.3% inserted it and delivered tidal volumes above 150 ml within 2 minutes. question: Endovenous laser ablation in the treatment of small saphenous varicose veins: does site of access influence early outcomes?
answer: In 59 patients undergoing EVLA for small saphenous vein reflux, access above versus below mid-calf did not produce significantly different early outcomes: complications (phlebitis 6% vs 3.8%; paresthesia 6% vs 19%, P=.223) and recurrence (9% vs 3.8%, P=.623) did not differ significantly. question: Will clinical studies elucidate the connection between the length of storage of transfused red blood cells and clinical outcomes?
answer: A simulation study found that the power of randomized trials to detect a link between RBC storage duration and clinical outcomes depends on how storage time is categorized, the temporal pattern of the storage lesion, and the age distribution of inventory. For most combinations of these factors, power was below 80%, so trials may often fail to clarify the connection. All four simulated trial designs had very low power to detect a harmful effect confined to the last week of the 42-day shelf life. One small randomized, double-blind trial in critically ill anemic patients compared RBCs stored ≤5 days with those stored ≥20 days and found no significant differences in gastric mucosal oxygenation or other oxygenation indexes.

question: Are increased carotid artery pulsatility and resistance indexes early signs of vascular abnormalities in young obese males?

question: Does the radiographic transition zone correlate with the level of aganglionosis on the specimen in Hirschsprung's disease?

question: Is there a model to teach and practice retroperitoneoscopic nephrectomy?
answer: Yes, a porcine model has been developed for retroperitoneoscopic nephrectomy training: fifteen piglets underwent standard three-port retroperitoneoscopic nephrectomy, and the model simulated the whole procedure from creating the working space to completing the nephrectomy. The model showed an experimental learning curve of about eight cases. Later cases (group B) had significantly fewer peritoneal openings (p=0.025), shorter operative time (p=0.0037), and less blood loss (p=0.026) than the first eight (group A). Operative times in the model ranged from 15 to 50 minutes (median 30) and blood loss from 5 to 100 mL (median 20). There were five peritoneal openings and two vascular complications, which were managed laparoscopically.

question: Could different follow-up modalities play a role in the diagnosis of asymptomatic endometrial cancer relapses?
answer: Different follow-up modalities did contribute to detecting asymptomatic endometrial cancer recurrences: among 165 asymptomatic patients, the first procedure prompting further work-up was imaging in 62.4%, clinical visit alone in 36.4%, and cytology in 1.2%. Detecting recurrence while asymptomatic was associated with longer survival from relapse (median 35 months vs 13 months for symptomatic recurrence, P = 0.0001), and vaginal vault recurrences had significantly longer survival than recurrences at other sites.

question: Regional anesthesia as compared with general anesthesia for surgery in geriatric patients with hip fracture: does it decrease morbidity, mortality, and health care costs?
answer: In a retrospective cohort of 308 hip fracture surgery patients, regional anesthesia (n=73) did not lower hospitalization costs compared with general anesthesia (n=235): $16,789 vs $16,815, P=0.9557. The same study found no statistically significant difference between the regional and general anesthesia groups in in-hospital mortality or readmission rates. Factors associated with higher costs or mortality were delay in surgery and ICU admission (costs), and age, male gender, African American race and ICU admission (mortality), rather than anesthesia type.

question: Does responsibility affect the public's valuation of health care interventions?
answer: In a UK online survey of 1030 people, the public's valuation of preventive interventions varied with who or what caused the harm: preventing hospital-acquired infections (health care responsibility) was valued more highly (1.31) than preventing genetic disorders (1.0). The effect was not uniform across health care-caused harms: drug administration errors were valued about the same as genetic disorders (1.07), and injuries to health care staff were weighted lower (0.71). Harms linked to individual responsibility were given less weight than genetic disorders, with lifestyle-related harms at 0.65 and sports injuries at 0.41.

question: Is vitamin D deficiency a feature of pediatric celiac disease?
answer: In biopsy-diagnosed celiac children aged 3-12 who were not yet on a gluten-free diet, serum 25(OH)D did not differ from non-celiac children (27.58 vs 26.20, p=0.59), so vitamin D deficiency was not a distinguishing feature in this cohort. Non-obese celiac children had similar 25(OH)D to non-obese controls (28.39 vs 30.64, p=0.52). Non-obese celiac children had higher levels than obese non-celiac children (28.39 vs 21.58, p=0.009), which may suggest obesity rather than celiac disease relates to lower levels, though this comparison does not test that directly. In a separate pediatric cohort, dietary vitamin D intake was deficient both before and after a gluten-free diet, and plasma vitamin D improved after one year on a gluten-free diet.

question: Type II supracondylar humerus fractures: can some be treated nonoperatively?
answer: Yes: in a prospective registry of 259 pediatric type II supracondylar humerus fractures, 150 (57.9%) were ultimately treated nonoperatively, and at final follow-up carrying angle change, range of motion, and complications did not differ clinically significantly between nonoperative and surgical groups. Fractures without rotational deformity or coronal angulation and with a shaft-condylar angle >15 degrees were more likely to be successfully managed nonoperatively, and patients with isolated extension deformity were more likely to complete nonoperative management successfully. A scoring system based on these clinical and radiographic features was developed to stratify injury severity and help identify which type II fractures may be suitable for nonoperative care.

question: Failed IUD insertions in community practice: an under-recognized problem?
answer: In a prospective observational study of copper T380A IUD insertion for emergency contraception at community family planning clinics in Utah, 35 of 197 insertion attempts (about 18%) were unsuccessful, even though the providers were experienced nurse practitioners. Failure was more frequent in nulliparous women (27/138, 19.6%) than in parous women (8/59, 13.6%), but the adjusted difference was not statistically significant (aOR 2.31, 95% CI 0.90-6.52, p=.09). The failures occurred without adjuvant measures for difficult insertions such as cervical anesthesia, dilation, pain medication, or ultrasound guidance.

question: Cardiovascular risk in a rural adult West African population: is resting heart rate also relevant?
answer: In a random sample of 574 adults from rural Ghana, elevated resting heart rate (>90 bpm) was present in 19% and was independently associated with higher odds of casual high blood pressure (OR 1.94, 95% CI 1.15-3.26) after adjusting for established CVD risk factors. Resting heart rate was also significantly associated with age, waist circumference and blood pressure in this rural Ghanaian population, in which 79% had at least one CVD risk factor. Resting heart rate showed reasonable within-person reproducibility on repeat measurements two weeks apart (regression dilution ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.62-0.89), supporting its use as a measurable marker.

question: Does feeding tube insertion and its timing improve survival?

question: Staging laparoscopy in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma: is it useful?
answer: In a retrospective series of 56 HCC patients, staging laparoscopy had a low yield: it showed unresectability in 4 patients (7.1%; overall yield 7%, 95% CI 3-17%), and accuracy was only 27%. Staging laparoscopy allowed biopsy of the contralateral non-tumorous liver in 45 patients, which changed management in 4 patients with cirrhosis. Six additional patients (13%) were found unresectable at exploratory laparotomy after laparoscopy, so some unresectable disease was still missed by staging laparoscopy.

question: Has the use of complementary and alternative medicine therapies by U.S. adults with chronic disease-related functional limitations changed from 2002 to 2007?
answer: Yes. Among U.S. adults with chronic disease-related functional limitations, overall use of 22 CAM therapies rose from 26.9% in 2002 to 30.6% in 2007 (unadjusted), and from 30.6% to 34.4% after age standardization (both p<0.001). Adults with limitations in changing and maintaining body position saw CAM use increase from 31.1% to 35.0% (p<0.01). Use of several specific therapies increased: deep breathing exercises (17.9% to 19.9%), meditation (11.0% to 13.5%), massage (7.0% to 10.9%), and yoga (5.1% to 6.6%). Use of the Atkins diet decreased (2.2% to 1.4%).

question: Juvenile osteochondritis dissecans: is it a growth disturbance of the secondary physis of the epiphysis?
answer: In a matched MRI study of 30 children with juvenile OCD and 30 controls, secondary physeal disruption was significantly more frequent in OCD condyles than in unaffected and control condyles (p<0.001), supporting the hypothesis that juvenile OCD is related to a disturbance of the secondary physis. OCD condyles also showed chondroepiphysial widening and subchondral bone edema compared with unaffected and control condyles (both p<0.001), whereas chondroepiphysial integrity and contour did not differ significantly between groups. All children in the study were skeletally immature, and lesions were located in the middle and/or posterior thirds of the condyle in the sagittal plane, mostly on the medial condyle (24 of 30 knees).

question: Does music influence stress in mechanically ventilated patients?

question: Do episodic migraineurs selectively attend to headache-related visual stimuli?
answer: Episodic migraineurs did not show selective attention to headache-related pictures: in a dot probe task, migraine status was unrelated to attentional bias for headache stimuli (F[1,306] = 0.56, P = .45), and there were no within-group reaction time differences between headache and happy conditions. question: Is obesity a risk factor for wheezing among adolescents?
answer: In the Pelotas birth cohort, obesity at age 11 was associated with about 50% higher prevalence of wheezing at age 15 compared with eutrophic peers (RR 1.53; 95% CI 1.14-2.05), independent of confounders. Obesity at age 11 was also associated with persistent wheezing through adolescence (RR 1.82; 95% CI 1.30-2.54), and higher skinfold tertiles at 11 years were linked to higher wheezing prevalence at 15 years (p = .011). Weight status and skinfolds were not associated with incident (new-onset) wheezing, so the risk appears to relate to wheezing prevalence and persistence rather than new onset. Among asthmatic 12- to 17-year-olds, obesity showed a trend toward greater airflow obstruction and asthma symptoms compared with nonobese asthmatics, which is directionally consistent.

question: Quaternary cytoreductive surgery in ovarian cancer: does surgical effort still matter?
answer: In a series of 49 relapsed epithelial ovarian cancer patients undergoing quaternary cytoreduction, achieving no tumour residual was associated with markedly longer mean overall survival than any residual disease (43 vs 13.4 months; P=0.001), suggesting surgical effort still matters. Postoperative systemic chemotherapy after quaternary cytoreduction was also associated with longer mean overall survival (40.5 vs 12.03 months; P<0.001) and had a significant protective effect in multivariate analysis. Multifocal tumour dissemination predicted incomplete resection, higher operative morbidity and lower survival, while ascites, platinum resistance, high grade and advanced age had no prognostic impact. Major operative morbidity was 28.6% and 30-day mortality 2%.

question: Is intensive chemotherapy safe for rural cancer patients?
answer: In a retrospective audit of 121 patients with node-positive breast and metastatic colorectal cancer, rural and urban patients given the same intensive chemotherapy had similar dose intensity (>95% for breast cancer) and similar serious adverse event rates, with no toxic deaths in either group. Febrile neutropenia occurred in 9.3% of urban versus 7.4% of rural patients (P=0.56), and diarrhoea and vomiting rates with XELOX did not differ significantly. Only two rural patients needed transfer to Townsville for admission. A teleoncology model in Mount Isa, supervised by the same oncologists as the tertiary centre, showed no significant differences from the tertiary centre (Townsville) in dose intensity, side effects, or hospital admissions, and no toxicity-related deaths in either group. In a prospective audit at a regional general physician-led centre in Albany, 8.33% of patients (1.47% of cycles) had neutropenic fever, and there were no deaths during the study period.

question: Is etoricoxib effective in preventing heterotopic ossification after primary total hip arthroplasty?
answer: In a prospective phase-2 study of 42 patients after cemented primary total hip arthroplasty, oral etoricoxib 90 mg for seven days was followed by no heterotopic ossification in 62% of patients at six months. question: Is the processing of affective prosody influenced by spatial attention?
answer: Spatial attention influenced the processing of affective prosody: ERP effects of emotional prosody interacted with spatial attention at early processing stages (<200 ms), while the two effects were additive at later stages (>200 ms). question: Does the type of tibial component affect mechanical alignment in unicompartmental knee replacement?
answer: In a retrospective review of 89 robotic-guided unicompartmental knee replacements, postoperative mechanical alignment was significantly closer to neutral with a metal-backed onlay tibial component (mean 2.8°) than with an all-polyethylene inlay component (mean 3.9°), after adjusting for gender, BMI, age, side and preoperative alignment (P=0.003). question: Is vancomycin MIC creep a worldwide phenomenon?
answer: In a Portuguese tertiary hospital, MRSA vancomycin MICs showed no consistent upward creep over 2007-2009: the share of isolates with MIC >1 mg/L fluctuated (86.2% in 2007, 93.3% in 2008, 58.8% in 2009; p=0.002), and no isolate had an MIC >2 mg/L. question: The colour of pain: can patients use colour to describe osteoarthritis pain?
answer: In group interviews with 17 patients with knee OA, the idea of using colour to describe pain was generally acceptable, and the majority thought they could use colour to describe their pain to healthcare professionals. Most participants chose red for high-intensity pain, associating it with inflammation, fire, anger and stop signals, while colours for no pain reflected positive feelings such as purity, calmness and happiness. Aching pain was consistently linked to grey or black, whereas sharp pain was described using a wider range of colours, and a range of colours was used to represent changes in pain intensity.

question: Are women with major depression in pregnancy identifiable in population health data?
answer: Women with depression in pregnancy are only partly identifiable in linked population health data: in Western Australia, antidepressant dispensing records captured 4.6% of pregnant women and hospital admission records captured 3.1%, but only 899 pregnancies (13.6% of cases) appeared in both sources. Ascertainment depended heavily on the data source: 80% of women dispensed an antidepressant had no depression comorbidity recorded in their hospital records. A capture-recapture estimate put prevalence at about 16%, well above what either source identified alone. Evidence from primary care suggests that medication records are also an imperfect marker of depression. Antidepressant prescription registration was the best single indicator but recognised only 43% of interview-confirmed depression, and combining indicators raised this to 69%.

question: School food policy at Dutch primary schools: room for improvement?
answer: Yes: a survey of Dutch primary schools found that although 87.1% of principals reported a written food policy, the rules were mostly not clearly defined, which points to room for improvement in policy content and implementation. Views on enforcement were mixed among parents: 28.1% thought the school should enforce the policy more strongly, 32.1% were satisfied, and 39.8% had no opinion. Teachers and principals saw parents as primarily responsible for encouraging healthy eating, whereas 49.8% of parents thought schools also share this responsibility, a gap in perceived roles that could be addressed.

question: Are intraoperative precursor events associated with postoperative major adverse events?
answer: In a matched retrospective cohort of low- to medium-risk cardiac surgery patients, at least one intraoperative precursor event was more frequent in patients with postoperative MACE (death, acute renal failure, stroke, infection) than in matched patients without MACE (33% vs 24%; P = .015). answer: In a retrospective series of 93 subjects with unexplained unsteadiness/gait impairment, orthostatic myoclonus was the most frequent EMG-identified disorder (16 patients, 17.2%), ahead of orthostatic tremor (13.9%) and low-frequency tremors during orthostatism (12.9%). question: Is the urinary biomarkers assessment a non-invasive approach to tubular lesions of the solitary kidney?
answer: In a cross-sectional study of 37 patients with solitary kidney (acquired and congenital), urinary biomarkers (NAG, alpha-1-microglobulin, albuminuria) were measured in urine and were frequently abnormal, supporting their use as a non-invasive way to assess tubulointerstitial lesions of the solitary kidney. In both acquired and congenital solitary kidney, NAG, urinary alpha-1-microglobulin and albuminuria correlated inversely with eGFR, and the biomarkers were significantly correlated with each other. Elevated NAG was found in 60.66% of acquired and 52.63% of congenital solitary kidney patients, whereas elevated alpha-1-microglobulin was less common (16.66% and 5.26%).

question: Preoperative platelet count in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma: is it a prognostic factor?
answer: In a retrospective analysis of 425 ESCC patients, preoperative platelet count was an independent prognostic factor on multivariate analysis (P = 0.013), alongside T grade and N staging. Patients with a preoperative platelet count ≤ 205 ×10^9/L had significantly better 5-year survival than those with a count >205 (60.7% vs. 31.6%, P<0.001). The survival difference was significant when lymph nodes were involved (32.0% vs. 12.7%, P = 0.004) but not when nodes were negative (68.6% vs. 58.8%, P = 0.085).

question: Does high blood pressure reduce the risk of chronic low back pain?
answer: In the HUNT study, higher blood pressure was inversely associated with low back pain: cross-sectionally, systolic, diastolic and pulse pressure were all inversely related to prevalence in both sexes, and prospectively in initially pain-free women, higher pulse pressure (OR 0.93 per 10 mm Hg) and systolic pressure (OR 0.95 per 10 mm Hg) predicted lower risk. question: Location and number of sutures placed for hiatal hernia repair during laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding: does it matter?
answer: In a retrospective analysis of 2,301 LAGB patients who had hiatal hernia repair, neither the number nor the location (anterior, posterior, or both) of sutures was associated with differences in band-related reoperation, 30-day readmission, or postoperative BMI/%EWL. Fewer sutures and anterior suture placement were associated with shorter operating time (1 suture 45 min vs. 4+ sutures 56 min; anterior 41 min vs. posterior 56 min vs. both 59 min). Posterior suture placement was associated with a longer length of stay than anterior or combined placement (84% staying 1 day vs. 74% for each of the other groups).

question: Is CA72-4 a useful biomarker in differential diagnosis between ovarian endometrioma and epithelial ovarian cancer?

question: Is there a first night effect on sleep bruxism?
answer: In a retrospective two-night polysmnographic study of sleep bruxism patients, no first night effect was found for most sleep variables, and the RMMA episode index did not differ between nights. Some measures did differ: total sleep time, sleep efficiency and stage transitions showed significant time-by-group interactions, and the second night had higher burst index, bruxism time index and mean burst duration. Five of 8 patients in the low-frequency group moved to the moderate-high frequency group on night two, while only 1 moved the other way, indicating night-to-night variability in classification.

question: Is the advanced age a contraindication to GERD laparoscopic surgery?
answer: Advanced age does not appear to be a contraindication to laparoscopic total fundoplication for GERD: in 620 consecutive patients, those aged 65 or older (n=96) had excellent outcomes in 88.9% versus 93.0% in younger patients (not statistically significant). question: Is the 7th TNM edition suitable for biological predictor in early gastric cancer?
answer: In 1,845 surgically treated early gastric cancer patients, the seventh TNM node staging was suitable as a biological predictor: upstaged IIA and N2/N3 categories were more strongly associated with aggressive features than the lower categories. Stage IIA (upstaged under the seventh edition) was more significantly associated with poor differentiation, signet ring cell, diffuse and undifferentiated types, perineural invasion, larger size and younger age than stage IB. In submucosal cancer, N2/N3 by the seventh staging was more significantly associated with larger size, poor differentiation, signet ring cell, diffuse and undifferentiated types, perineural invasion and deeper submucosal invasion. In mucosal cancer, N2/N3 was associated with younger age and diffuse and undifferentiated types.

answer: In a retrospective analysis of California and Florida EDs, HIE participation was associated with a lower probability of repeat imaging at unaffiliated EDs within 30 days across all three modalities studied: CT (-8.7 percentage points), ultrasound (-9.1), and chest x-ray (-13.0). The comparison was between 37 EDs that began HIE participation and 410 that did not.

question: Prevalence of chronic conditions among Medicare Part A beneficiaries in 2008 and 2010: are Medicare beneficiaries getting sicker?
answer: Medicare Part A beneficiaries had more chronic conditions on average in 2010 than in 2008, indicating a modest deterioration in average health. The increase in average number of chronic conditions was larger for dual-eligible beneficiaries (2.8%) than for nondual-eligible beneficiaries (1.2%). Trends differed by condition: prevalence of congestive heart failure, ischemic heart disease, and stroke/TIA decreased, while chronic kidney disease, depression, diabetes, osteoporosis, and rheumatoid arthritis/osteoarthritis drove the overall worsening.

question: Are we seeing the effects of public awareness campaigns?
answer: In this South West melanoma series, the proportion of thin (0-1 mm) melanomas at first presentation rose year on year from 2003 to 2012, with a significant positive linear trend (p<0.0001). This is consistent with a shift toward earlier presentation after awareness campaigns. The proportions of 1-2 mm and 2-4 mm melanomas fell significantly (p=0.0013 and p=0.0253), while thick melanomas (>4 mm) showed no significant change (p=0.1456).

question: Is there a relationship between serum paraoxonase level and epicardial fat tissue thickness?
answer: Serum PON 1 was significantly lower in patients with epicardial fat tissue thickness ≥7 mm than in those with <7 mm (168.9 vs 253.9 U/L, p<0.001), which indicates an inverse relationship at this threshold. The continuous analysis found no significant linear correlation between epicardial fat thickness and serum PON 1 (r = -0.127, p=0.069), although the direction was negative. Higher epicardial fat thickness (≥7 mm) was also associated with greater hypertension prevalence and higher serum triglyceride, and body mass index was higher in the ≥5 mm group.

question: Delayed imaging in routine CT examinations of the abdomen and pelvis: is it worth the additional cost of radiation and time?
answer: In a retrospective review of 1000 routine abdominopelvic CT scans, delayed phase imaging added information in only 4.2% of patients and gave no benefit in 95.8%, so it appears not worth the added radiation. Most delayed-phase-only findings were incidental (liver hemangioma, adrenal adenoma, parapelvic renal cysts) and could have been confirmed with noninvasive follow-up imaging such as sonography or unenhanced CT or MRI. The most important finding was a single renal mass (0.1% of patients) seen only on delayed images, while the delayed phase raised mean effective radiation dose by 59.5%.

question: Is nasogastric decompression useful in prevention of leaks after laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy?
answer: In a prospective randomized study of 145 sleeve gastrectomy patients, nasogastric decompression did not prevent staple line leaks: one leak (1.4%) occurred in the nasogastric tube group and none in the group without a tube. Routine nasogastric tube placement was also associated with a significantly longer postoperative hospital stay (7.6 vs 6.2 days, p=0.04), with comparable operative time and blood loss between groups.

question: Pharmacologic regimens for knee osteoarthritis prevention: can they be cost-effective?
answer: A simulation model found that DMOAD prophylaxis for knee OA can be cost-effective only under limited conditions: in a high-risk cohort (obese with prior knee injury), the base case regimen gave an ICER of $118,000 per QALY gained. In lower-risk groups the regimen was not cost-effective: ICERs exceeded $150,000/QALY in the knee-injury-only cohort, and the regimen was less cost-effective than standard of care in the obese-only and no-risk-factor cohorts. Cost-effectiveness depended heavily on price: regimens priced at $3,000 per year or more had ICERs above cost-effectiveness thresholds consistent with current US standards.

question: Is crime associated with over-the-counter pharmacy syringe sales?
answer: In Los Angeles Police Department Reporting Districts from 2006 to 2008, OTC pharmacy syringe sales were not associated with higher reported crime; after adjustment, crime rates were negatively associated with OTC syringe sales (adjusted rate ratio 0.89; 95% CI 0.81, 0.99). question: Is lumbar drainage of postoperative cerebrospinal fluid fistula after spine surgery effective?
answer: In a series of 16 postoperative CSF fistulas after spine surgery, the 10 patients treated with external lumbar CSF drainage for ten days all healed their wounds properly with no adverse events, with a mean cure time of about 10 days. Lumbar drainage cured fistulas faster than conservative management (prone positioning for three weeks), which took a mean of about 30 days, although all patients in both groups healed.

question: Are high flow nasal cannulae noisier than bubble CPAP for preterm infants?
answer: In an observational study of preterm infants, HFNC was not noisier than bubble CPAP: average noise at the external auditory meatus did not differ significantly (mean difference -1.6 dBA, 95% CI -4.0 to 0.9 for HFNC vs BCPAP). At low frequency (500 Hz), HFNC was about 3.0 dBA quieter than BCPAP (95% CI 0.3 to 5.7). Noise rose with increasing BCPAP gas flow (p=0.007) but not with set pressure, and there was a trend toward higher noise with increasing HFNC gas flows.

question: Does SYNTAX score predict in-hospital outcomes in patients with ST elevation myocardial infarction undergoing primary percutaneous coronary intervention?
answer: In 538 STEMI patients undergoing primary PCI, a high SYNTAX score (>22) was associated with worse in-hospital outcomes than a low score, including higher reinfarction (9.5% vs 7.3%, p=0.037) and mortality (0.9% vs 0.2%, p=0.021). question: MR arthrography of the shoulder: do we need local anesthesia?
answer: Skin local anesthesia before intraarticular contrast injection for shoulder MR arthrography did not reduce pain: in 249 patients, mean VAS was 2.6 with anesthesia versus 2.6 and 2.7 in two control groups (p=.960). A second patient survey (n=74) likewise found no difference in arthrography injection pain between those who received local anesthetic (mean VAS 20.8) and those who did not (19.3; P=0.83). Pain perception differed between men and women (p=.009), but the sex difference was equal across the anesthesia and no-anesthesia groups (p=.934), so sex did not alter the lack of an anesthetic effect.

question: Does ethnicity affect where people with cancer die?
answer: Yes: in a study of 93,375 cancer deaths among Londoners aged 65 and over, place of death differed by country of birth (used as a proxy for ethnicity) even after adjustment, with time-consistent gaps persisting across groups over 2001-2010. After adjustment, hospital deaths were more likely for those born in Asia (PR 1.12) and Africa (PR 1.11), and hospice deaths were less likely for those born in Asia (PR 0.73), Africa (PR 0.83) and 'other' regions (PR 0.90). Home deaths were less likely for those born in the Caribbean (PR 0.91). Home deaths rose and hospital deaths fell over the decade across several groups, but the differences between groups remained.

question: Is dexamethasone an effective alternative to oral prednisone in the treatment of pediatric asthma exacerbations?
answer: A review of six pediatric clinical trials found that prednisone was not superior to dexamethasone for mild to moderate asthma exacerbations, and a meta-analysis showed no difference between the two in symptomatic return to baseline or unplanned physician revisits after the initial emergency department visit. Some of the included studies found additional potential benefits of dexamethasone, including better compliance and less vomiting, with a shorter course of 1-2 days compared with the usual 5-day prednisone/prednisolone course.

question: Undescended testes: does age at orchiopexy affect survival of the testis?
answer: In a retrospective review of 349 testes, age at orchiopexy was not significantly associated with postoperative atrophy once testis location was adjusted for (p=0.055). Overall postoperative atrophy occurred in 7.7% of testes. Unadjusted, atrophy was highest with orchiopexy at 13-24 months (12%, 16 of 133) compared with under 13 months (5%, 3 of 64) and over 24 months (5%, 8 of 152) (p=0.0024). This pattern was not monotonic with age. Intra-abdominal testis location, not age, was the independent predictor of atrophy. The odds of atrophy were 15.66 times higher for abdominal than inguinal testes (95% CI 5.5-44.6).

question: The association of puberty and young adolescent alcohol use: do parents have a moderating role?
answer: In a cross-sectional survey of 7631 Australian adolescents aged 10-14, parent-adolescent emotional closeness, family conflict, and parental permissiveness did not moderate the puberty-alcohol use association: interaction terms between family factors and pubertal stage did not improve model fit. question: Is oncoplastic surgery a contraindication for accelerated partial breast radiation using the interstitial multicatheter brachytherapy method?
answer: In a retrospective analysis of 134 patients (136 breasts) who had oncoplastic breast-conserving surgery for low-risk breast cancer, adjuvant APBI (HDR or pulse-dose-rate brachytherapy) was delivered with low recurrence rates, which argues against oncoplastic surgery being a contraindication. After a median follow-up of 39 months, local events were few: 2 different-quadrant in-breast tumors among 89 HDR patients and 1 local recurrence among 45 PDR patients; 131 of 134 patients were alive. Late toxicity was mild, with fibrosis in 27 breasts, hyperpigmentation in 14, telangiectasia in 6, and keloid formation in 1.

question: Medical student education in emergency medicine: do students meet the national standards for clinical encounters of selected core conditions?
answer: Most students did not meet the full national standard: in a 4th-year EM clerkship, only 15.4% of 130 students saw all 10 CDEM-recommended core conditions, though 76.9% saw at least eight. question: Assessing joint line positions by means of the contralateral knee: a new approach for planning knee revision surgery?
answer: Measuring distances from bony landmarks to the joint line on the contralateral knee appears to be a viable way to assess the natural joint line: in 100 patients (200 knees), the mean difference in fibular head-to-joint-line distance between the treated and control knee was 0.0 mm (confidence limits -1.1 to 1.1 mm). The approach rests on the inherent bilateral symmetry of the body, and the authors propose it because assessing joint lines from bony landmarks alone is inadvisable given large anatomical variation between individuals.

question: Does government assistance improve utilization of eye care services by low-income individuals?
answer: Program design may help explain this. Assistance requires receipt of social assistance, which has stringent criteria and reaches only 5.5-7.9% of older Canadians, while 12.5-13.2% report difficulty paying for basic expenses. Coverage of costs is incomplete in many provinces. Assistance fully covers a routine eye exam in only 5 provinces and is insufficient in the rest, and eyeglass assistance is inadequate in 5 provinces, requiring out-of-pocket copayments.

question: Can common carotid intima media thickness serve as an indicator of both cardiovascular phenotype and risk among black Africans?
answer: In a black African (Nigerian) sample of 456 people, common carotid IMT differed significantly across stroke, hypertensive and normotensive phenotypes bilaterally (p<0.001), and it was the only factor that correlated significantly with all the traditional cardiovascular risk factors assessed. question: Can routine offering of influenza vaccination in office-based settings reduce racial and ethnic disparities in adult influenza vaccination?
answer: A national survey of US adults found that unvaccinated racial and ethnic minorities had more "missed opportunities" for influenza vaccination in office-based settings than non-Hispanic whites. Eliminating these missed opportunities could have cut racial and ethnic disparities in vaccination by roughly one half. In US nursing homes, racial vaccination gaps between African American and Caucasian residents were smaller (<6 percentage points) and nonsignificant where facility-wide strategies such as standing orders, verbal consent, or routine review of vaccination rates were used. Gaps were two to three times as large in homes without these strategies.

question: Emergency double-balloon enteroscopy combined with real-time viewing of capsule endoscopy: a feasible combined approach in acute overt-obscure gastrointestinal bleeding?
answer: In a retrospective series of 27 patients with severe overt obscure GI bleeding, emergency DBE (within 24 h) combined with real-time capsule endoscopy viewing was feasible. Lesions amenable to hemostasis were found in 23 patients and 21 of them (77.8%) were treated successfully. Emergency DBE detected Dieulafoy's lesions significantly more often than DBE done more than 24 h after symptom onset (40.7% vs 0.9%, P < 0.001). Real-time capsule endoscopy viewing, used in 16 of the 27 patients, correctly modified DBE management in four of them (25%).

question: Reporting and interpreting red blood cell morphology: is there discordance between clinical pathologists and clinicians?
answer: Surveys of 1662 small animal clinicians and 82 clinical pathologists found areas of both agreement and discordance in how red blood cell morphology terms are reported and interpreted. Both groups considered some terms (e.g., agglutination) useful, but only pathologists found others (e.g., ghost cells) useful. All groups interpreted some terms (e.g., Heinz bodies) correctly, whereas some clinicians misinterpreted others (e.g., eccentrocytes). Pathologists often do not report morphologic changes they consider insignificant when present in low numbers. Also, 28% of clinicians believe pathologists review all blood smears, whereas only 19% of pathologists report doing so.

question: Did Chile's traffic law reform push police enforcement?
answer: The Chilean study describes a police traffic enforcement increment registered after the 2005 traffic law reform. This is consistent with the reform being followed by greater enforcement. question: Is there a correlation between androgens and sexual desire in women?
answer: In a cross-sectional study of 560 healthy women, sexual desire correlated overall with calculated free testosterone and androstenedione. In women aged 25-44 years not using systemic hormonal contraception, sexual desire correlated with total testosterone, free testosterone, androstenedione, and DHEAS; in women aged 45-65, only androstenedione correlated with desire. The androgen metabolite androsterone glucuronide (ADT-G) showed no correlation with sexual desire, so it was not a better marker than circulating androgens.

question: Does airway surgery lower serum lipid levels in obstructive sleep apnea patients?
answer: In a retrospective review of 113 OSA patients, upper airway surgery (nasal surgery or UPPP) was followed by significant decreases in serum total cholesterol and lipoprotein(a), although HDL, LDL and triglycerides did not change significantly overall. The lipid effects varied by surgery type: after UPPP, TC, HDL and Lp(a) improved, whereas after nasal surgery only Lp(a) decreased. Effects also varied by baseline lipid status: patients with normal baseline lipids showed only an Lp(a) decrease, while those with isolated hypertriglyceridemia improved in HDL, TG and Lp(a), and those with mixed hyperlipidemia showed decreases in TC and LDL.

question: Do elderly patients call 911 when presented with clinical scenarios suggestive of acute stroke?
answer: Most elderly outpatients in Buenos Aires did not correctly endorse calling 911 for stroke scenarios: only 14% met the ≥75% correct-response cut-off on the Stroke Action Test. Even with the most typical stroke signs and symptoms, only 65% said they would call an ambulance. On average the correct response was chosen only 37% of the time, and for amaurosis fugax only 15% would call. Higher education was associated with correct endorsement of calling 911 (secondary school adjusted OR 3.53; tertiary/university adjusted OR 3.04, relative to lower education).

question: Is it possible to stop treatment with nucleos(t)ide analogs in patients with e-antigen negative chronic hepatitis B?
answer: Stopping nucleos(t)ide analogues was possible for some HBeAg-negative CHB patients but not others. Among 22 patients who discontinued NA therapy with normal ALT/AST, undetectable DNA and no cirrhosis, 12 (54.5%) had virologic relapse, so about 45% kept a sustained response. Relapse came early: the mean interval to relapse was about 6.4 months, and 75% of relapses happened within 12 months of stopping. This suggests close monitoring is needed in the first year after discontinuation. Patients with a sustained response were older on average and had received longer treatment than those who relapsed, but these differences were not statistically significant. The study therefore did not identify who can safely stop.

question: Can emergency physicians accurately and reliably assess acute vertigo in the emergency department?
answer: In a prospective ED study of 98 patients with isolated vertigo, trained emergency physicians using the STANDING protocol identified central causes with 92.9% sensitivity and 96.4% specificity against senior audiologist evaluation (13 true positives, 3 false positives, 81 true negatives, 1 false negative). Inter-observer agreement among emergency physicians was good for the whole STANDING test (kappa 0.76), with step-wise kappas of 0.86 (spontaneous nystagmus), 0.93 (nystagmus direction), 0.73 (head impulse test) and 0.78 (gait). The physicians had limited experience in nystagmus assessment, and the evaluation took about 9.9 minutes on average (range 6-17 min).

question: Do preoperative serum C-reactive protein levels predict the definitive pathological stage in patients with clinically localized prostate cancer?
answer: In a prospective study of 629 patients with clinically localized prostate cancer undergoing radical prostatectomy, preoperative CRP was not associated with a locally advanced tumor stage, lymph node metastases, or positive surgical margin on uni- or multivariate analysis. CRP showed only a limited link to tumor grade: patients with Gleason score ≥8 had higher median CRP than those with ≤7 (1.9 vs. 1.2 mg/l, p = 0.03), but multivariate analysis relativized the association between elevated CRP and poor differentiation. CRP also did not correlate with initial PSA level or clinical tumor-associated findings.

question: Do Web-based and clinic samples of gay men living with HIV differ on self-reported physical and psychological symptoms?
answer: Web-based and clinic samples of gay men with HIV differed on psychological symptoms: the Web sample had worse mean psychological symptom burden (1.61 vs 1.36) and, after adjustment, higher odds of being in the worst symptom tertile (adjusted OR 2.20, 95% CI 1.41-3.44). Physical symptom burden was similar between the samples (mean 0.78 Web vs 0.70 clinic), and recruitment setting was not significantly associated with high physical symptom score after adjustment. Being in paid employment was associated with lower odds of being in the worst tertile for both physical (adjusted OR 0.41) and psychological (adjusted OR 0.32) symptoms. The Web sample was younger, more likely to be employed, and less likely to be on antiretroviral therapy than the clinic sample.

question: Is minimally invasive mitral valve repair with artificial chords reproducible and applicable in routine surgery?
answer: In a retrospective review of 426 consecutive patients, neochordal repair was used routinely in all patients undergoing video-assisted minimally invasive mitral repair, with a 99.8% repair rate and 1.2% 30-day mortality. question: Does Residency Selection Criteria Predict Performance in Orthopaedic Surgery Residency?
answer: Some preresidency selection criteria predicted orthopaedic resident performance: in a 60-resident single-institution review, USMLE Step 2 scores and number of clinical honors correlated moderately with ABOS Part I scores (r=0.55 and r=0.45) and weakly with OITE scores (r=0.29 to 0.35). AOA membership was associated with higher faculty global evaluation scores, most strongly in the interpersonal and communication skills subsection. In a four-program study of 181 residents, USMLE Step 1 scores correlated with ABOS Part I performance (r=0.53), and OITE scores correlated at an average of 0.50 with ABOS Part I, with correlation increasing from PGY2 to PGY5. Residents averaging in the 27th percentile or lower on the OITE had a 57% chance of failing the ABOS Part I examination.

question: 30-Day and 1-year mortality in emergency general surgery laparotomies: an area of concern and need for improvement?
answer: A retrospective study of 446 patients undergoing emergency laparotomy found substantial mortality, with 30-day mortality of 12.4% in patients under 70 and 22% in those over 70, and 1-year mortality of 25.15% and 38% respectively, supporting that this is an area of concern. Mortality rose significantly with age: both 30-day and 1-year mortality were higher in patients over 70 than in those under 70 (p<0.001 for each). question: Does base deficit predict mortality in patients with severe traumatic brain injury?
answer: In a retrospective study of 108 patients with isolated severe TBI, base deficit on admission did not predict mortality: mean BD did not differ significantly between survivors and non-survivors, and the area under the ROC curve for BD as a mortality predictor was non-significant. Admission base deficit did show a weak but statistically significant negative correlation with presenting GCS (r = -0.239) and Revised Trauma Score (r = -0.214), so it is related to injury severity at presentation even though it did not predict death.

question: Is there a connection between sublingual varices and hypertension?
answer: In an observational study of 431 dental patients, medium/severe sublingual varices were associated with hypertension (OR = 2.25, p<0.002). Sublingual varices indicated hypertension with a positive predictive value of 0.5 and a negative predictive value of 0.80.

question: Is Aspiration Thrombectomy Beneficial in Patients Undergoing Primary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention?
answer: In a meta-analysis of 17 randomized trials (20,960 STEMI patients), aspiration thrombectomy before primary PCI did not significantly reduce mortality (2.8% vs 3.2%; RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.76-1.04) or reinfarction (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.73-1.17) compared with conventional PCI. Aspiration thrombectomy also showed no significant benefit on the combined outcome of mortality or reinfarction (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.79-1.02) or on stent thrombosis (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.62-1.08). Aspiration thrombectomy was associated with a nonsignificant trend toward more stroke (0.6% vs 0.4%; RR 1.45, 95% CI 0.96-2.21). Meta-regression found no modification of the effect on mortality, reinfarction, or their combination by use of intravenous glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors or by ischemic time.

question: Can biofeedback training of psychophysiological responses enhance athletes' sport performance?
answer: An 8-week biofeedback program in 18 athletes (vs 21 controls) led more experimental-group athletes to control psychophysiological parameters under stress, with significant differences only for some measures. These included GSR regulation (p=0.037), heart rate after the Stroop stressor (p=0.037), and heart rate-breathing coherence after the math stressor (p=0.042). The study aimed to test whether biofeedback enhances athletic performance, and it questioned experimental-group athletes one year later about continued skill use and perceived performance gains. The reported results do not give any performance outcome.

question: Does the clinical presentation of a prior preterm birth predict risk in a subsequent pregnancy?
answer: In a retrospective cohort of 522 women with a prior spontaneous preterm birth, the clinical presentation of that birth predicted recurrence: recurrent preterm birth occurred in 55.2% after prior advanced cervical dilatation, versus 27.2% after PPROM and 32.2% after preterm labor (P = .001). Women whose prior preterm birth presented with advanced cervical dilatation also delivered earlier in the subsequent pregnancy (mean 34.0 weeks vs 37.2 weeks for prior PPROM and 37.0 weeks for prior PTL) and had significantly shorter lowest cervical lengths before 24 weeks.

question: Does patient-prosthesis mismatch after aortic valve replacement affect survival and quality of life in elderly patients?
answer: In elderly patients receiving small (19 or 21 mm) aortic prostheses, patient-prosthesis mismatch (indexed EOA <0.85 cm²/m²) did not affect survival: 5-year survival was 78 ± 4.5% and was not influenced by PPM in one study, and survival at 58 months was 81 ± 6.4% with no PPM effect (p = 0.9845) in another. Quality of life did not differ by PPM status: RAND SF-36 scores in PPM patients were similar to those of no-PPM patients, and SF-12 testing showed no differences between groups in the second study. Functional status improved even with PPM, with mean NYHA class in long-term survivors with PPM improving from 3.0 to 1.7 (P < 0.001). In the multivariable Cox analysis, only preoperative NYHA class, not PPM, was an independent risk factor for late death.

question: Can nurse-led preoperative education reduce anxiety and postoperative complications of patients undergoing cardiac surgery?
answer: In a randomised trial of 395 elective cardiac surgery patients, nurse-led preoperative education reduced state anxiety the day before surgery (34.0 vs 36.9; P=0.001) and produced a greater decline in state anxiety over follow-up than standard information. Education and admission trait anxiety were independent predictors of reduction in state anxiety in multivariate regression. question: Pap smears with glandular cell abnormalities: Are they detected by rapid prescreening?
answer: Rapid prescreening detected only a minority of glandular cell abnormalities: of 107 smears with a final interpretation of ≥AGC, 39 (36.4%) were flagged for review on RPS. Among 71 patients with histologic follow-up, 24 had HSIL or carcinoma, and 13 of those 24 Pap smears (54.2%) had been flagged on RPS. RPS also picked up 11 AGC cases that full screening missed, 2 of which showed endometrial adenocarcinoma on follow-up, so RPS added some detection value as a QA step despite its limited sensitivity.

question: Eyelid-parotid metastasis: do we screen for coexisting masses?
answer: A case series found that eyelid tumours can metastasise to the parotid gland and vice versa: two patients with malignant parotid tumours later developed eyelid lesions histologically similar to the primary, and a third had ipsilateral upper eyelid and parotid tumours. This supports checking the parotid when an eyelid tumour is found, and the eyelid when a parotid malignancy is found. The authors used histology and immunocytochemistry to distinguish the primary tumour from the metastasis in coexisting eyelid and parotid masses. Separately, a retrospective parotidectomy series found synchronous multiple tumours within the same parotid specimen in 14 of 341 patients, so more than one mass can coexist within the gland itself.

question: Does evidence-based practice improve patient outcomes?
answer: In a natural experiment in a hospital internal medicine service, the evidence-based practice (EBP) unit had lower mortality (6.27% vs 7.75%) and shorter length of stay (6.01 vs 8.46 days) than standard practice patients, with no difference in patient complexity or admissions. Within the EBP unit, mortality fell from 7.4% to 6.3% and length of stay from 9.15 to 6.01 days relative to its own pre-reorganization performance, while standard practice physicians showed no significant improvement. Readmission rates were similar between the EBP and standard practice units (14.4% vs 14.5%), so the benefit was not seen across all outcomes.

question: After CLASS--Is a voluntary public insurance program a realistic way to meet the long-term support and service needs of adults with disabilities?
answer: A national survey suggests a voluntary public PAS insurance program would have limited realistic viability: although 26.7% of adults aged 40-65 (25.8 million) expressed interest, only 1.8% (1.6 million) would pay $100 or more per month. question: Target Serum Urate: Do Gout Patients Know Their Goal?
answer: Most gout patients did not know their serum urate goal: in a survey of 612 Veterans Affairs gout patients on allopurinol, only 14% knew their SU goal. Knowledge of the SU goal was much lower than knowledge of other gout topics, since the majority of patients answered correctly on the other 5 gout-specific knowledge questions. Having a rheumatologist as the initial prescriber (OR 3.0) and answering all other 5 knowledge questions correctly (OR 2.1) were associated with greater odds of knowing the SU goal. SU goal knowledge was associated with self-reported global health status, but not with self-reported health-related quality of life or gout-specific health status.
